items.title: Deser: Rethinking Rust Serialization
items.content_html:
Serde is an amazing serialization library for Rust and it has been a huge reason why I felt productive with it for years. However already while at Sentry I got quite frustrated with some of the limitations with it but actually replacing Serde is tricky because of the might that it has in the ecosystem. Also because it’s quite hard to actually do better without also making some potentially painful compromises.

Here are three examples of Serde corner cases that show poor interactions of Serde features or unexpected limitations:

A number that is a map

An internally tagged enum, with serde_json‘s arbitrary_precision feature turned on:

#[derive(Deserialize)]
#[serde(tag = "type")]
enum Shape {
    Circle { radius: f64 },
}

serde_json::from_str::<Shape>(r#"{"type": "Circle", "radius": 1.5}"#)
// error: invalid type: map, expected f64

Serde’s data model has no place for arbitrary precision numbers, so serde_json uses in-band signalling with a map with a magic key. The enum has to buffer the fields until it has seen the tag, and the buffer does not know about the magic key. Because Cargo features are unified, it’s enough for any crate in your dependency graph to turn the feature on.

Flattening breaks integer keys 
#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct Stats {
    scores: HashMap<u32, u32>,
}

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct Report {
    name: String,
    #[serde(flatten)]
    stats: Stats,
}

serde_json::from_str::<Report>(r#"{"name": "x", "scores": {"42": 23}}"#)
// error: invalid type: string "42", expected u32 at line 1 column 35

Stats on its own parses {"scores": {"42": 23}} just fine. JSON keys are always strings, and serde_json only turns them into integers if the type asks for one. However once flatten buffers the value, "42" is just a string. The error also points at the end of the document rather than at the key.

Adapters do not compose 
fn from_hex<'de, D: Deserializer<'de>>(d: D) -> Result<u32, D::Error> { ... }

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct Theme {
    #[serde(deserialize_with = "from_hex")]
    primary: u32,
    #[serde(deserialize_with = "from_hex")]
    accent: Option<u32>,
}

//error[E0308]: `?` operator has incompatible types
//  |
//  |     #[serde(deserialize_with = "from_hex")]
//  |                                ^^^^^^^^^^ expected `Option<u32>`, found `u32`
//  |
//help: try wrapping the expression in `Some`
//  |
//  |     #[serde(deserialize_with = Some("from_hex"))]
//  |                                +++++          +

A function cannot be passed as a type parameter, so there is no way to apply from_hex to the inside of an Option, a Vec or a map. You write another function for every wrapper, and once you have from_opt_hex the field is no longer optional unless you also remember to add #[serde(default)].

None of these are bugs that are easy to fix in Serde. They fall out of its design, and that design is protected by Serde’s stability guarantees.

Back in 2022 I started an experiment called Deser. It’s a serialization library for Rust that takes the user experience of Serde and puts it on top of a completely different architecture inspired by miniserde. I never really finished it and it sat around for a few years. I picked it back up, and it has now reached a point where I think it’s worth looking at. Even just to inspire others to see if they want to explore the space.

The Name And Idea

The name is Serde with its two halves swapped. Deser is Serde but the other way around. In Serde, a type drives the deserialization process: a Deserialize impl asks the deserializer for the kind of value it expects, the format calls back into a visitor. Every nested value is handled by recursion which makes Serde deserialization inherently grow the stack with each level of nesting.

Deser on the other hand turns this around and the format tells the type of the next value and pushes events into a sink. When a sink hits the start of a nested value, it doesn’t call into it but hands back a new sink to a driver, which keeps all state on the heap (in fact, in an arena). On the way out, emitters return their nested values instead of recursing into them.

That also means that Deser cannot support formats like protobuf that are not self describing. They are in fact quite intentionally left out of the design entirely. Which is one way to say: if you want to “fix” Serde, you need to make some other compromises.

Most of the reasons for Deser’s ideas go back to Sentry Relay, which processes enormous amounts of untrusted JSON. Over the years when I was at Sentry we ran into the same set of problems again and again, and many of them are not really bugs in Serde but consequences of its design. Serde’s stability guarantees mean that a lot of them cannot be fixed without breaking every format and every hand written implementation. Most of these problems come from three decisions:

  1. One set of traits for all formats. Serde serves both self describing formats (JSON, YAML, TOML, …) and formats where the reader has to know the type upfront (postcard, bincode, protobuf, …). That is incredibly useful, but it means that some features only work with some formats, and you find out at runtime. In case of Serde it also has some odd wrinkles where a derived struct quietly accepts an array in place of an object in JSON for instance.

  2. A fixed data model that loses information when buffering. Internally tagged enums, untagged enums and flatten need to buffer values before they know what to do with them. The buffer can’t hold everything the format knew, errors lose their location and extensions to the ecosystem rely on in-band signalling to express things such as arbitrary precision numbers.

  3. Recursion on the call stack. Every level of nesting uses stack space. Formats protect against this with a recursion limit, but the moment you go through a code path that doesn’t have one (writing, dynamic values), deeply nested data can take down your process. It also means that a deserialization cannot be paused while you wait for more input.

Many of the corresponding Serde issues have been open for years, and I wrote about abusing Serde before. People have tried different angles on this over the years. Some went minimal and dropped most features to get fast compiles and no recursion. dtolnay’s own miniserde is the best example of that, and deser’s trait design was originally modelled after it. Other recent attempts went for runtime reflection, or for a new data model with a focus on binary formats.

If you want to read up on all of the collected challenges with Serde’s design, I maintain a lengthy list here.

Dethroning Serde

First of all I don’t think it’s likely that one can replace Serde. The orphan rule entrenches Serde incredibly well in the ecosystem. But some things are within the reach of a crate author’s control. In case of Deser it’s completeness.

Deser today implements all important self describing formats from YAML, JSON, TOML, CBOR, JSON5 and the likes, but also XML and plist to really close the gap. XML in particular is something Serde has declined to support, and it shows (more on that below). At the very least format support should not be the reason not to use Deser.

The second problem usually is that actually solving Serde’s issues comes at a significant cost in compile time and/or runtime performance. Deser is no different. While Deser’s compile times are a bit better than Serde’s, the binary bloat is quite a bit worse and the runtime performance is mixed. It’s roughly comparable if you look at the numbers but depending on the format structure you are losing significantly from some of the tradeoffs.

That said, it’s now in a state where it’s at least in principle a drop-in replacement where the tradeoffs might work well for users.

Deser’s Design

Deser does not try to be significantly different than Serde on the surface level. For most uses you derive Serialize and Deserialize and then start using it with your format implementing crate of choice. Most attributes are very similar, though they are taking Rust expressions instead of strings.

use deser::{Serialize, Deserialize};

#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[deser(rename_all = "camelCase")]
pub struct Account {
    id: u64,
    account_holder: String,
    #[deser(default)]
    is_deactivated: bool,
}

let account: Account = deser_json::from_str(json)?;

The difference in the design would become more apparent if you implement a serializer or deserializer yourself. Instead of visitors that call into each other recursively, deserializing a type creates a sink which receives events that are directly emitted by the parser, and serializing produces emitters that hand out values. Nested sinks and emitters are handed back to a driver, which keeps them on the heap. This design, which is entirely stolen from miniserde, gives some interesting consequences:

  • No stack overflows. You can arbitrarily nest structures without issues. For untrusted input you set limits with a layer, and you pick the number that you are comfortable with, which is independent of your stack space.
  • Suspendable. Because the state lives in the driver, a deserialization can be fed input as it arrives. It’s also Send, so it can move between threads while you wait on IO which makes it much nicer to use with tokio. Formats like JSON, CBOR and MessagePack can be parsed as a stream if you so desire.
  • An extensible data model. The core data model is small and made of atoms, maps and sequences. For all else, there are extension values (DateTime, Uuid, etc.) that also all carry a fallback for formats that don’t understand them. Unlike Serde this means it does not rely on in-band signalling of objects with magic keys to smuggle values through.
  • Lossless buffering. When a value has to be buffered (for instance because the tag of an internally tagged enum comes last), Deser records the events together with everything the format knew about them. Protocol specific extension types or error locations all survive.
  • Layers are a middleware system that sit between the format and your types and can track things like paths, enforce safety limits, rename keys or redact values without having to touch specific code paths.
  • Native flattening that doesn’t buffer at all.

On top of that are a lot of things that I just wanted to have:

  • Allow enum tags to be of any type, not just strings
  • Adapters that compose (as = Option<Vec<DisplayFromStr>>)
  • Enabling validation as an adapter
  • derive attributes that are real Rust expressions instead of strings
  • bytes as a core functionality in the data model
  • duplicate keys rejected by default and errors that point at the problem

Here is a small configuration type that shows a few of these together:

use deser::adapters::DisplayFromStr;
use deser::de::Recording;
use deser::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use deser_encoding::Hex;
use deser_validate::{Check, NonEmpty, Range};
use ipnet::IpNet;

#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct Config {
    // at least one 256-bit key, each written as hex
    #[deser(as = Check<NonEmpty, Vec<Hex>>)]
    secret_keys: Vec<[u8; 32]>,
    // `IpNet` knows nothing about deser, but has `FromStr` and `Display`
    #[deser(as = Option<Vec<DisplayFromStr>>)]
    allowed_networks: Option<Vec<IpNet>>,
    listeners: Vec<Listener>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[deser(tag = "type", rename_all = "snake_case")]
pub enum Listener {
    Unix { path: PathBuf },
    Tcp {
        host: IpAddr,
        #[deser(as = Check<Range<1, 65535>>)]
        port: u16,
    },
    // types this version does not know are kept and written back
    #[deser(other)]
    Other(#[deser(tag)] String, Recording),
}

Adapters are types, so Hex can go inside a Vec, and DisplayFromStr inside a Vec inside an Option. Validators are adapters too, so Check<NonEmpty, Vec<Hex>> decodes the keys and then checks that there is at least one. The catch-all variant keeps the tag and a recording of everything else in case someone wants to process it later.

Errors are something I care a lot about, so here is what happens when a value is wrong:

secret_keys = ["9f86d081884c7d659a2feaa0c55ad015a3bf4f1b2b0b822cd15d6c15b0f00a08"]
allowed_networks = ["10.0.0.0/8", "fd00::/8"]

[[listeners]]
type = "unix"
path = "/run/app.sock"

[[listeners]]
host = "127.0.0.1"
port = 0
type = "tcp"

[[listeners]]
type = "quic"
host = "::1"
alpn = ["h3"]

let config: Config = deser_toml::Deserializer::from_str(input)
    .deserialize_with(|driver| driver.push_layer(PathLayer::new()))?;

Note that here the tag of the internally tagged enum comes last which means that the values have to be buffered until the tag is known. In Serde this is tricky and we would lose the location if we used some tricks to add it. With Deser however, with the path layer enabled Deser you where in the structure the problem is:

Unexpected: invalid value: must be between 1 and 65535 at line 10 column 8 (path: listeners[1].port)

Deser Meta Data

Deser really wants to be extensible, and XML is a more extreme example of the differences between Deser and Serde. Here is an Atom entry that mixes in Dublin Core for the authors:

use chrono::{DateTime, Utc};
use deser::Deserialize;
use deser_value::Value;
use deser_xml::DeserializerConfig;

deser_xml::namespace!(
    atom = "http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom",
    dc = "http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/",
);

#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
struct Entry {
    #[deser(rename = atom!("title"))]
    title: String,
    #[deser(rename = dc!("creator"))]
    creators: Vec<String>,
    #[deser(rename = atom!("updated"))]
    updated: DateTime<Utc>,
}

// entries we understand, and everything else is kept as it is
#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
#[deser(untagged)]
enum Item {
    Entry(Entry),
    Other(Value),
}

let item: Item = DeserializerConfig::new()
    .resolve_namespaces(true)
    .from_str(r#"
        <entry xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom"
               xmlns:d="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
          <title>Deser</title>
          <d:creator>John</d:creator>
          <updated>2026-09-29T21:00:00Z</updated>
          <d:creator>Jane</d:creator>
        </entry>
    "#)?;

XML uses namespaces which means that names need to be matched by their namespace, not by the prefix the document happens to use. Here the document says d: and the type says dc!. atom!("title") is just the string {http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom}title, which works because attributes are expressions. The two creators are collected into one Vec even though there is another element between them, and the text of updated goes straight into a chrono datetime. Because the enum is untagged, the entry has to be buffered before a variant is picked, and deser’s buffer keeps both creators. So the result is an Entry with John and Jane.

quick-xml, the most popular XML crate for Serde, drops the prefixes and ignores namespaces entirely, so a <x:title> from some other namespace is happily accepted as the title of the entry. The split list part though is considerably worse. A plain Entry fails with a duplicate field error for creator, unless you turn on the overlapped-lists feature (which, remember, is a global additive flag that any crate could set). That feature makes quick-xml read ahead to the end of the element and buffer everything in between, without a limit unless you set one.

But the feature only helps when quick-xml is hooked up to the struct directly and no buffering is taking place. Wrap the struct in the untagged enum and Serde buffers the entry itself. Read from that buffer, Entry sees creator twice and fails again. The fallback is a map, which keeps only the last creator, and there is no error. With or without the feature you get this:

Other({"creator": {"$text": "Jane"}, "title": {"$text": "Deser"}, ...})

Notice how John is gone.

Format specific extension types such as TOML datetimes are another case. TOML has them natively, Serde’s data model does not, so the toml crate passes them on as a map with a magic key. In Deser a datetime is an extension value, which formats that know it keep and all others write as a string:

let value: Value = deser_toml::from_str("released = 2026-09-29T21:00:00+02:00")?;

deser_json::to_string(&value)?;
// {"released":"2026-09-29T21:00:00+02:00"}
deser_toml::to_string(&value)?;
// released = 2026-09-29T21:00:00+02:00

The same with serde_json::Value gives you {"released":{"$__toml_private_datetime":"2026-09-29T21:00:00+02:00"}}, and reading the value into a chrono::DateTime fails outright with invalid type: map, expected an RFC 3339 formatted date and time string.

The Cost

So now that you know Deser is at least in theory cool, at what cost?

It is not free. The design relies on dynamic dispatch and on sinks and emitters that live on the heap, and that has considerable runtime overhead. In my own measurements for JSON, Deser reads somewhere between 33% faster and 60% slower than serde_json depending on the data. On average it’s about 10% slower for reading. Writes are between three times as fast and 70% slower and a wash on average. For YAML and TOML it’s noticeably faster than the Serde based crates, but that is more about the format implementations than the architecture.

Compile times slightly are better, but not dramatically so. Because it doesn’t monomorphize everything, release builds of derived code are about 2.3 times as fast as with Serde and that get a tiny bit better in practice for your own code as less recompilation is necessary.

To make Deser’s design work at all, it also uses unsafe internally. Most of this is to keep the chain of borrowed sinks on the heap. I feel like this is fine in the days of Miri and agents, but I know it makes some folks uneasy.

And well, the biggest cost is that it’s just not Serde.

How Much Is There?

Quite a lot actually which might be surprising. In addition to the core there is support for derive.

It supports all flavorts of JSON you can think of: JSON, JSONC, JSON5 and HJSON. (Fun fact here: they are all generated out of one shared parser template) For binary handling it supports CBOR and MessagePack. Additionally it does YAML 1.1 and 1.2, TOML, XML and all three flavors of Apple’s plist as well as CSV/TSV, urlencoded data and environment variables. For more crazy contraptions you can attach path info or capture location data as well as support for debug printing. You can perform validation as you parse, opt into different binary encodings in addition to base64, you can bridge to serde or capture dynamic values, transcode between formats or hook it up with tokio.

For documentation see docs.rs/deser and the code itself is on GitHub alongside many examples.

items.title: Stop f*cking trying to feel confident
items.content_html:
Share

You can’t think your way to confidence.

Confidence isn’t a feeling either. And waiting to be confident is absolute stupidity. Confidence definitely isn’t a personality trait or something you’re born with.

The mystery around what real confidence is messes people up for decades. Most never learn the secret to real confidence before they die.

The way confidence works is far simpler.

It’s based on psychology and neuroscience. And once you understand how true confidence works, your life will never be the same again. You will do things you never thought you could do (even if you’re shy or an introvert).

Give me 4 mins. This will change your life.

A Stanford psychologist accidentally shared how to become dangerously confident

Psychologists have spent decades studying differences between confident and unconfident people. None of them could accurately figure it out.

That was until psychologist Albert Bandura became obsessed with figuring it out. And what he found out is incredible. Anyone can become confident if they’re willing to make one small change. You need to understand the background first though.

Albert did 100s of experiments with confident and unconfident people. Then he wrote down why some people were insanely confident and have aura, while other people were ignored and perceived as worthless. He also looked at why some people crave doing hard things while others avoid doing them, made excuses, or just stood still.

One huge finding stood out.

Confident people don’t magically f*cking avoid doubt. He found confident people had just as much doubt as everyone else. What gave confident people extreme confidence was what he labelled self-efficacy.

To understand it, let me share an experiment he ran. Albert split a room of people with similar skills and experience into two groups. He then gave them a difficult task. Before they could work on the task, he told Group 1 they had nailed tasks like this before and should do well. He told Group 2 they sucked at tasks like this in the past.

The results were shocking.

Group 1 performed insanely well and recovered from failure, rejection, and embarrassment much faster. Group 2 gave up much sooner even though they had the same skills and experience. Tragic.

Here’s what this means for you…

Your brain doesn’t gain confidence from BS, woo-woo positive thinking – or even affirmations – because you can’t think your way to confidence. No.

Your brain generates confidence from a proven track record of doing hard things and surviving. Each tiny win creates more momentum and leads to more confidence.

Every time you smash through feelings of doubt or uncertainty, instead of hoping it’ll go away, your brain makes a note. It logs the event as evidence.

Every time you give the speech in public, start the business, publish the essay, ask the guy/gal out, or take the promotion… every time you do the hard, uncomfortable thing instead of avoiding it, your brain is freaking paying attention like an FBI agent. And each time your brain updates its algorithm and prediction on what you might be able to achieve.

Insanely confident people are no different from you.

They’ve just repeatedly given their brain a lot of evidence that they can do hard, uncomfortable things more than you have. It’s not more complicated than that, which means you can quickly become more confident if you want. Like, right now.

It’s taken me 40 years to realize that confidence is the cheat code to life

I have never been a confident person.

In school I got bullied, hard. I never went to university. Women ignored me for most of my adult life (maybe it was the big ears). But I was even less confident than you might think. When I faced extreme mental illness 5+ years ago, things got even darker.

I didn’t just have rock bottom confidence. My lack of confidence was sabotaging my every move. All I had was a brain full of evidence that everything would go wrong.

I became so anxious I didn’t have the confidence to sit in a meeting room with the door closed because I didn’t trust myself not to vomit.

This may sound like a small thing, but it wasn’t.

I couldn’t do job interviews. I couldn’t have meetings with a boss. I couldn’t even go to the doctor. By the end, I couldn’t even sit in a chair and get my hair cut, so I was forced to have long hair. The boys called me Barbie because of my long, blonde, girly hair and would greet me with “Hey, babe.”

It was hell.

It got even worse. All the anxiety turned into an eating disorder. Every birthday celebration I’d eat my birthday dinner at a restaurant with my family, then vomit it all up in the bathroom about halfway through.

Do you know what that does to your confidence?

Well, you have negative confidence. You start to not even trust the ground you walk on. That was me. So in case you think you lack confidence, you’re probably nowhere near as bad as I was.

But I accidentally learned this little brain hack by myself.

I decided one day to see if I could produce evidence that was the opposite. I wrote down a list of every fear I had. Things such as flying on planes, giving a speech, sitting in a meeting room, and going on a date with a girl.

Then I committed to tackling just one item on the list.

I chose what I thought was the easiest one: going up a few floors in an elevator. I chose the Sofitel building in downtown Melbourne, Australia.

I got into the elevator hoping I’d be alone in case anything went wrong or I shat myself. Just as the door was closing, a husband and wife entered the elevator. My palms started sweating.

I went as white as a ghost.

Instead of panic, I turned it into a video game. I thought to myself, “How cool would it be if I could somehow pull this off?” After a few minutes the elevator stopped and I jumped out. I’d made it! I was so excited I jumped back in the elevator a few minutes later and went back down. I got a high from it. I became addicted.

I went back to the list and picked another item: flying on a plane for 2 hours. I booked a ticket to Sydney. I got on the plane. I was terrified but also thrilled.

The stakes here were higher because if my anxiety took over there was no asking the pilot to land the plane mid-air. I once again turned it into a video game.

I imagined defying the odds and winning. And I accepted the downside of a full-blown panic attack with the flight attendants having to resuscitate me mid-air. Things didn’t go to plan.

Once again I was unlucky.

The most popular kid from my high school happened to be on the same plane. He recognised me and said hello. Then he sat right near me. I now had a witness. The embarrassment factor skyrocketed. But again, I just disconnected from the outcome and thought about what winning would do.

And I won. Again. No issues.

For the next few years, I worked my way through every item on the list. I did job interviews for the hell of it. I asked for promotions. I started doing public speaking at Toastmasters. By the end of the experiment I was…

  • Giving speeches at the Toastmasters State Championships, and giving talks to rooms full of 100s of my banking colleagues

  • Building a side business teaching people how to write online

  • Travelling all over the world to places like Vietnam, Italy, Spain, and Japan

  • Doing interviews on major podcasts with people like Dan Koe

  • Getting promoted to Director-level roles in big companies

  • Posting on social media to millions of followers

  • Going on dates with supermodels (no joke)

  • Leading teams of ten or more people

(Contrast this with the guy who couldn’t sit in a room with the door closed.)

I don’t say any of this to brag because I know you don’t give a f*ck. I tell you this because there’s a hidden pattern.

Just like Dr Albert Bandura, I found that the more evidence I gave my brain that I could do hard things, the more confident I became.

By the end of the experiment, I became insanely confident. My confidence is now so high people from my childhood, high school, and even former employers don’t recognize me. The same people I used to look up to are now asking me quietly in DMs for help.

It’s not because I’m brilliant. It’s because I hacked my brain using neuroplasticity and the secret to real confidence that Dr Albert Bandura figured out. The only difference was I didn’t know about his experiment back then, and only discovered it recently.

You, too, can literally do and achieve anything when you have real confidence.

Real confidence isn’t knowing you’ll win

That’s just what people mistakenly think.

I’ve learned the hard way that real confidence is knowing you can come back from failure, rejection, and embarrassment no matter what happens.

Real confidence is being optimistic. It’s being relentless. It’s being able to pivot and iterate. It’s being able to deal with uncertainty and not need to have all the answers.

Real confidence is knowing that even if the worst-case scenario happens, it’s never the end. You can come back from anything. It’s knowing that whatever problem, struggle, or challenge you face, you’ll f*ck around and figure it out.

Just like with investing, the secret to winning is being okay with the downsides while remaining focused on the eventual upside if you stay in the game.

Most people don’t realise confidence comes from practice. The more you do, the less you doubt – Raj Shamani

Where most people go wrong with building confidence

Confidence without evidence is delusion.

The average person wants to be confident, but doesn’t take the action needed to produce evidence of results. When your brain has no evidence of results, it has no choice but to create self-talk that makes you doubt yourself.

This logically makes sense.

What changes is when you understand the power of neuroplasticity at a 5th-grader level. Neuroplasticity means your brain is like my 3-year-old daughter’s purple playdough. It changes shape every time you practice or learn something new.

So the more you do something, the stronger those neural pathways get.

To become more confident, you need to first take the actions that produce results, create evidence, and slowly rewire your brain. Your brain isn’t easily fooled. You can’t think your way to confidence. You must prove it to your brain through basic action.

Closing Thought

Give your brain evidence that you can do hard things.

That’s the secret to real confidence that you’ve been searching for your entire life. Start with small actions to build momentum, then slowly increase the intensity.

Let neuroplasticity work in your favor, too, rather than work against you. That’s how you become insanely confident and do things you never thought you could do in a million years.

P.S.

Possibly the question I get asked most frequently online is:

“I have this business idea... but will it make money?”

Good news. You don’t have to guess.

All you have to do is watch my latest YouTube video.

items.title: Maybe you're just an outlier
items.content_html:
Share

Outliers are secret weirdos.

They live a life most people don’t understand. I’ve been lucky to work with many outliers. Some of them became generational high performers. One-in-a-million types that do things most of us can’t even comprehend.

I’ve been fascinated with outliers ever since Malcolm Gladwell wrote the book Outliers. And I’ve applied his learnings to try and spot outliers, because I believe working with and encountering an outlier is a life-changing experience. Some of their awesomeness always seems to rub off on me.

It’s uncomfortable for me to say this, but I have probably become an outlier.

The thing about outliers is they are hard to spot. Here are the signs you’re not broken but are in fact just an outlier.

You’ve experienced untold trauma

In mainstream society, trauma and tragedy get a bad rap.

Most people use it as an excuse. “I can’t do X Tim because bad things happened to me, dontcha know.” So they become a victim, assign a label to their condition, and take meds to make the pain go away. That’s a completely normal reaction. No judgement there. I can see why people do it. But…

I’ve never aligned with this mainstream view.

I’ve always seen trauma and tragedy as an amplifier. Truthfully, as a 20 year old, I hoped I would experience pain, tragedy, and heartbreak. I shouldn’t admit this but I even craved it. And don’t worry, I got a lot of it.

For several decades, I hit rock bottom so many times it felt normal. Each time I imagined myself as Batman in the movie “The Dark Knight” trapped in the bottomless pit of a prison with a bunch of psychos trying to escape.

And like a true loony, I loved it.

When I lost everything multiple times, I smiled. When I had $1.2M stolen from me in 30 minutes back in 2021, I saw it as an advantage. When multiple long-term romantic relationships blew up after I joined a religious cult, it inspired me to be better.

The chance you come from a poor family, rack up millions of followers, hit 1B+ content views, build an email list of almost 400K subscribers, and make millions of dollars online is statistically low. So much of what I’m sharing here makes perfect sense to me because I’ve lived it.

Turns out I’m not alone. Research suggests (study 1 + study 2) that moderate adversity, rather than a charmed and frictionless start, is a common thread among outliers. Enough hardship to forge resilience, but not so much that it breaks them.

Instead of the pain creating more pain, outliers use pain as an advantage.

Their brains are wired a little differently.

A great example of an outlier is my accountant. His family were part of the royal family in Vietnam. When the Vietnam War broke out his family lost everything after they lost the war. They escaped on 8 boats headed for Australia. Only one boat successfully made it to Australia carrying his mother and father. Pirates captured the other 7 boats during their voyage.

Those boats had no living survivors.

When his parents arrived in Australia, they took on massive debt. Then his father walked out and left his mother with nothing plus the huge debt.

They became homeless.

For all of his childhood and teenage life, he was homeless with his mother. They lived in homeless shelters like it was normal.

But it messed with my accountant’s brain.

He wanted to break the curse from a young age. So at school he became top of his class. Then he became top of the state in high school. Then he hit top of the country. He studied so hard he became a genius. Entering the workforce gave him enormous graduate opportunities.

By a young age he built his own business. He now owns multiple businesses doing tens of millions in revenue and a huge property empire.

His family will never be poor again.

When my accountant told me this story, I had tears in my eyes. It broke me. I felt goosebumps all over my body. He’s an incredibly inspiring human. Becoming his client was so obvious to me. That’s the energy of an outlier. It moves people to action and shows regular humans what’s possible.

Trauma can make or break you. For outliers, they experience trauma and use it to ensure they and their family never experience similar trauma again.

You follow the “Three Extremes Rule”

This formula comes from Aura startup founder Zach Pogrob.

1. Extreme focus (1 thing)

An outlier is someone who has achieved a hard goal.

They stand apart from the norm and achieve results that are so extreme it lands outside what is typical. Outliers are the geniuses, superstars, icons, and leaders the world looks up to.

To outperform in any field you must have extreme focus. It sounds obvious yet most people don’t do it. The average person spends most of their day looking at a smartphone that is nothing more than a casino slot machine.

This takes up most of their time, so they claim they are busy, when in reality they’re just distracted.

Outliers are the opposite. They spend an unreasonable amount of time focused on one thing. Not ten things. One thing.

They don’t have a to-do list or a goal list because what they must do is so blindingly obvious. For me, that means writing like a psychopath and publishing more work on social media than almost anyone else. My focus looks like “write a lot.”

2. Extreme timeline (1 decade)

Most people think short term.

They want money now. They want the Lambo now. They’re focused on the next person they can have s*x with. Outliers are the opposite. They have extreme timelines. They think in decades.

For example, when I started writing on the internet in 2014, I decided to dabble. I was going to try it out. But instead of trying it out for one month or one week, I chose the bizarre timeframe of 10 years. Same with public speaking. When I committed to the craft, I set myself a timeframe of at least 10 years.

Eventually I hit the top 1% in both (not to brag because you don’t care).

Longer timeframes produce better results. They show real commitment. You can’t learn much good or achieve any mastery in a week. But even if you’re normal IQ like me, you can definitely achieve a lot in 10 years.

Extend your time horizon to have more patience and achieve true mastery.

3. Extreme iteration (1% better, every day)

Malcolm Gladwell’s book spread a bullsh*t lie known as the 10,000-hour rule.

And while time in the game is important, most people mistake this rule. It’s why people have 20 years’ experience in their job but still make $50K a year.

If all you have is “years of experience” without extreme iteration, you ended up taking one year of work and learning… and repeating it for 20 years in a row.

That’s dumb.

Outliers do plenty of hours but they also do stupid numbers of iterations on their work, idea, or goal. Why? Because the definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over and expecting a different result.

Yet that’s how most people live.

They repeat the same boring actions, work hard, and don’t get ahead because they left out extreme iteration.

Extreme iteration is how you experiment, A/B test, learn, and acquire true wisdom.

It’s hard for normal people to iterate and change because their ego gets in the way. The factory-worker education system teaches them to believe they are always right. They can’t comprehend that they might be wrong. And they’re not willing to accept it.

And they don’t change because change is uncomfortable, and right now, we’re living through a comfort crisis. Multiple generations of humans that experience a tiny bit of stress, then quit and think they’re smart and justified (even empowered LOL).

When things get hard normal people quit and call it stress. But when outliers do hard things, they see it as learning and iterate their way to breakthroughs.

There is a downside though.

If you iterate and change too much, it becomes shiny object syndrome. You spend your life chasing false gods, cults, and rainbows looking for a magical solution that doesn’t exist. But if you don’t iterate enough, you learn nothing and think you’re the smartest person in the room.

The formula for iteration is 1% better each day. Small iterations without deviating from the plan or quitting a goal too soon.

You make people uncomfortable and even sweat

Outliers don’t tell you what you want to hear.

They’re not a people-pleaser who will lick your butthole and tell you how great you are. A conversation with an outlier is uncomfortable though. You feel on edge, yet they don’t insult you or say rude stuff. But there is a level of intensity.

They have standards and there’s a subtle pressure and assertiveness.

They’re a little unhinged too. Not so unhinged they sound like a conspiracy theorist, but not so aligned with mainstream culture that they’re a choir boy and part-time boy scout who can’t think for themselves.

It looks and sounds like “John was definitely no BS.”

The no BS is a filter they see the world through. They tell people how it is to save time and get to the point. It creates a slight aura around them and builds trust faster.

It feels authentic and genuine too, which is appealing in a world of fake leaders, politicians, and big corporations doing evil while pretending to do good. They hear feedback and listen, but they call out contradictory behavior and misaligned views.

Being challenged is how we all grow. And outliers can help you do that.

You chase genuine obsession at the risk of looking like a maniac

Most people are lukewarm passionate.

Outliers have transcended to the next level. One outlier I worked with in finance is a good example. On the outside he looked like a normal guy. But he wasn’t. In his spare time he read every piece of financial news he could. In between meetings, he was looking at trading screens and doing financial modelling.

He was already rich so it wasn’t for the money.

He was just obsessed with finance. At a young age, his father made him read the Financial Times every morning.

He started looking for good property investments as a teenager. He had a financial model for exactly what a good property should yield and where it should be located.

While other investors shouted “location, location, location,” he looked at state-level economic data. As an adult, he started buying homes up. He’d look at 300 properties in person before even buying one. His desk was full of town planning papers and population growth numbers for the last 100 years.

His obsession for finance transcended the normal constraints.

When I questioned him about it, he said none of it felt like work.

What he does during work hours and while he’s on holidays or enjoying the weekend looks exactly the same. Finance was a jigsaw puzzle. It kept him endlessly fascinated. There was no end to the game. Only mastery and pure obsession.

I asked him if he had a plan B in case finance didn’t work out. He looked at me like I’d just shat on his desk and slept with his wife. He was disgusted. He saw no existence where he’d be doing anything else.

It had to work. He’d force it to work.

Obsession cannot be beaten. It’s a form of transcendence.

You must prove an enemy wrong

Outliers have a chip on their shoulder.

Not in an angry Karen way. But as a form of quiet rage. The golf course swinging small d*ck that fired me for no reason is one of my enemies.

So are the intellectuals who refused to let me into higher education. As are the gatekeepers who run and operate the pointless corporate ladder that leads nowhere.

An outlier doesn’t let anger take over.

No. Instead, they desire to prove their enemy wrong. To show them through proof of work and results that they were wrong about them.

This is a powerful form of motivation. It’s forced me to get resourceful and do things I otherwise wouldn’t have done. I still remember a recruiter from Oracle 5 years ago who said “Tim, the reason you’ve been unemployed for 6 months is because you’re sh*t.” She alone probably made me at least $5M.

Funny thing is she got made redundant herself right after that and took a “career break” because she probably couldn’t get a new job either.

Having people doubt you is a powerful form of motivation.

You have an eccentric personality

Outliers are weirdos.

Last week I took my kid to the miniature train. We went on the small Thomas The Tank Engine one that was full of children aged between 2 and 5. The train goes like 3 mph. As we got off the tiny train, I recognized the driver.

He’s a well-known guy in the business world. He’s had a lot of success. Been part of many huge mergers and acquisitions. And he was driving a f*cking kids’ train on a Sunday. I pulled him aside. He remembered me from my banking days.

Dude just liked miniature trains. He’d been driving them for 20+ years.

I wish this was a new realization. But it’s not. I’ve seen this repeatedly. Outliers are quirky. They have odd personalities. Their houses are full of things you’ve never seen before. They collect strange stuff. They have hobbies most wouldn’t understand.

When they go to networking events or parties, they struggle to connect. They don’t know how to act normal and ask painful questions like “Soooo….how’s the weather?”

Many of them have non-linear career paths too.

They didn’t get a job at McDonald’s serving fries then eventually become the McDonald’s CEO.

I still remember another outlier I worked with who went from being a journalist in the Middle East, to a banker, to a farmer, to C-level exec, to an entrepreneur. His entire career history looks like one you’d find in the kids’ TV show Bluey (I watch it every day with my kiddo).

Linear careers equal boring.

Outliers are too weird to follow the traditional path to nowhere.

Closing Thought

If you want to spot the outlier in you, look for the strange stuff you do in the shadows, the non-obvious things nobody around you does. What you do doesn’t fit any framework or 10 steps to success model.

You won’t just learn from outliers. You’ll realize you were one all along.

When you embody the traits of an outlier, you have a more exciting life, a non-linear career, and you produce results you wouldn’t have been able to achieve any other way.

Fitting in is massively overrated. Channel the weird witchcraft of outliers.

items.title: Once you understand pattern recognition your life will never be the same again
items.content_html:
Share

It’s easy for you to get fooled over and over again.

That’s what it means to be human.

You try to achieve the same goal multiple times and fall short. No matter what you do the result doesn’t seem to change. It’s frustrating as hell…

And it’s why a lot of people give up.

There’s a simple solution though: Master pattern recognition. Learn to see the patterns in everything, so you can exploit them for your benefit. One of the greatest teachers of our time Tony Robbins says “There are certain patterns that are universal.”

Tony first saw this when he wanted to write a book about investing. Even though Tony has never worked on Wall Street or been a hedge fund manager, he interviewed ten of the greatest minds in the finance industry. He studied them.

By the end of writing his first book on investing, he saw patterns that all of these greats were doing without realizing it. That book is called “Money: Master the Game.”

That one book quietly changed the trajectory of my life — but not in the way you'd guess. I'll show you exactly how later.

Pattern recognition is a skill that gives you an unfair advantage. It lets you enter a new field, or go from being a beginner to a master much faster. Every skill, career, goal, or business can be figured out with the hidden skill of pattern recognition.

Mastering pattern recognition will change your life forever.

The ice cream truck driver who saw the pattern everyone else called "random"

In 1984, Michael Larson was an unemployed ice cream truck driver in Ohio.

No fancy degree. No millions in the bank. No talent anyone could point to. Just a fat man, a couch, and a VCR.

Like a loser, he got hooked on a CBS game show called Press Your Luck. The setup was simple: contestants stopped a board of flashing lights to land on cash, while praying they didn’t hit the “Whammy”.

Everybody assumed the board was random.

Everybody except Michael.

While the rest of America watched the show with a beer in hand, Larson recorded every episode and did something psychotic. He sat there with the remote and paused the tape. Frame. By. Frame. For weeks. Like a fat caveman version of a data scientist, hunched over a TV, hunting for something nobody believed was there.

And he found it.

The “random” board wasn’t random at all. It cycled through just five repeating patterns. Five. That was the whole secret.

He also figured out that two specific squares never held a Whammy and handed you a bonus spin every time. If he could hit them on command, he could run the board basically forever.

So he memorized all five patterns and drilled his timing until he could stop a spinning board on the exact square he wanted, on cue, like a sniper. Then he spent all his ice cream truck savings on a flight to LA to audition for the TV show.

A contestant supervisor was suspicious and didn’t want to let him on, but a producer overruled him. Michael looked like a harmless hillbilly from Tennessee.

Michael got on stage and wowed the audience.

He did dozens of spins in a row and didn’t get a single Whammy. The audience lost it. The host got twitchy. In the control room, CBS executives watched in slow-motion horror as this random ice cream truck guy calmly dismantled their show.

When Michael finally stopped, he’d won $110,237. It was the biggest one-day haul in game show history at the time.

CBS was pissed. They refused to pay.

They launched an investigation and studied the tapes for cheating.

And found nothing. Because there was no rule against paying attention. They paid him every cent, quietly reprogrammed the board, and buried the episode for nearly two decades so nobody would get any ideas.

An unemployed man with a VCR beat a national television network at its own game. Not with money. Not with connections. Not with luck.

With a pattern everyone else was too lazy to see.

The 5th-grader explanation of pattern recognition (so you can actually use it)

Pattern recognition is your brain’s ability to see the invisible structure underneath the noise.

Where everyone else sees chaos, randomness, or a pile of unrelated facts, you see a shape you’ve seen before. And you instantly know what it means and what’s coming next.

Here’s the part that’ll mess with you: pattern recognition is not intelligence. It’s not a gift. It’s not some magic third eye you’re born with.

Pattern recognition is compressed experience.

Every “intuitive” genius you’ve ever admired is really just running a massive database in the background.

Take chess. Sit a grandmaster in front of a board mid-game, let them look for 5 seconds, then take it away. They can rebuild the entire position from memory, almost perfectly.

Superhuman, right?

Except do the same thing with pieces scattered randomly across the board — a position that could never happen in a real game — and the grandmaster does no better than you or me.

Read that again.

Their “photographic memory” vanishes the second the pattern disappears.

Because they were never memorizing pieces. They were seeing familiar shapes, formations they’d seen 10,000 times before. Where a beginner sees 25 individual pieces, the master sees 5 or 6 meaningful groups. Same board.

Completely different resolution.

That’s the whole thing. Pattern recognition is what turns 10,000 hours of experience into a single glance. It feels like intuition. It’s actually a library. And once you understand that, the good news hits you: a library is something you can build.

The quiet pattern that changed my life, made me a millionaire, and allowed me to quit banking forever

I want to share a secret with you. I’ve never shared this before, so allow me to be vulnerable.

On the outside, I look like some lucky Aussie that won the internet lottery, got millions of followers, and retired on a beach with a hot wife and 2 kids.

This is a lie.

I hinted that pattern recognition changed my life. Let me share how. Before, I told you the Tony Robbins book in 2014 helped me see patterns. After I finished the book I became high as a kite on the idea of pattern recognition.

I felt euphoric. I felt like I’d opened Pandora’s box.

I thought to myself that people spend their entire life to make money. It occupies so much of their time. But if money truly was nothing more than a game full of patterns, then if I, Timothy Denning, could master it, perhaps I could win too.

I realize what I just said sounds delusional but that’s how I thought. I spent the next few years reading every book about money and Wall Street to recognize the patterns.

One night I found a glitch. Here it is…

Every one of us gets paid in a currency issued by a government. I studied history and noted that time and time again every empire in existence exploited its currency. It was too tempting not to. So if every government in history will always destroy their currency, then what does that say about money?

I realized my entire life I worked my butt off to earn this currency. I traded my precious time for it. So understanding the pattern of money had a huge payoff.

And I found the pattern.

Every government creates money from nothing through money printing. The more they print money the more all assets/investments rise in price. So as long as I invested money in the right things, the rise in money supply would inflate my investments.

I saw a pattern that some investments got inflated more than others. But no matter what, the pattern was obvious. From 2014 onwards I exploited this pattern, and it made me enough money to never work again.

Sure, I had some business success. I built a following. But the pattern that actually saved my life was understanding the pattern of how money is created.

If you’re willing to find the pattern, you can literally crack the code to any wild goal, outcome, or business.

The most important pattern in the history of the world

Here’s the pattern that runs the world:

Good times create weak people.
Weak people create bad times.
Bad times create strong people.
Strong people create good times.

Once you understand this pattern you can handle uncertainty like a Jedi master. You can face hard times in the middle of winter and know that bikini-babe summers are right around the corner.

This pattern gives you a quiet confidence. It’s one of the few patterns that explains the entire world in 4 sentences.

That’s how powerful patterns are.

They can take a complex topic like human history with infinite stories and data points, and compress them down to one 30-second insight. Mind blown? Mine is. Excuse me while I go to the dunny (joking not joking). Let the pattern of guaranteed good times fuel your optimism and help you achieve any goal.

You either see patterns, or you become a slave to subconscious patterns

It’s time to get a little dark.

This ain’t all lollipops and Kinder surprises. Karen in the comments needs to say “This Tim guy said he likes dead babies” before the real breakthrough happens. So here it is. Let’s get Karen in the comments fired up.

The best tactics are a paradox. Pattern recognition can change your life, but underneath, patterns can also ruin your life too.

Mastering pattern recognition did allow me to reach modern freedom. But failing to see patterns held me back for years before that. Some will choose not to see patterns. They will say pattern recognition is bullsh*t. But everything runs on patterns.

You either choose to see patterns and master the skill, or unconscious patterns will shape your life and you’ll call it bad luck, racism, discrimination, being neurodivergent, unhealed trauma, or some other BS.

Psychologist Carl Jung said it this way:

Until you make the unconscious conscious, it will direct your life and you will call it fate.

You must make the unconscious patterns conscious. This is simple but not easy. Most people are slaves to unconscious patterns.

Addictions are nothing more than unconscious patterns. You can stop jerking off to boobies or quit vaping if you really want to – but you won’t until you see the unconscious pattern.

For example, I had an addiction to junk food. I noticed whenever I felt anxious, I’d eat to relieve stress. So I took up the habit of meditation, became more chill, then I didn’t feel the need to down 7-Eleven slurpees by the gallon.

It wasn’t an eating problem. It was an anxiety problem.

When I faced extreme poverty I saw another pattern. Every time I found an opportunity, I sabotaged myself by focusing on all the downsides and being obsessed with risks instead of ROI.

This kept me stuck at $50K a year for longer than I care to admit.

On the surface, it looked like an earning problem. Or a generational issue I inherited because I came from a poor family. But it wasn’t.

It was a series of deeply limiting beliefs that made every million-dollar opportunity look like a brown bear looking for a human lunch and some hairy legs to munch.

The victim mindset is perhaps the greatest destroyer of human potential in existence.

When bad things happen or tragedy strikes, the unconscious pattern of becoming a victim takes over. Instead of “I can change this,” we go to “this happened to me and now I can’t live a good life again.”

One perspective is empowering, the other one is a prison sentence served in a pool full of quicksand surrounded by beer bros smoking cigarettes yelling “There’s no way out Timmy Boy!”

The neuroscience technique high performers have known about for 100s of years

I’m not a psychologist. I didn’t study neuroscience.

But when I first encountered Tony Robbins’ work I learned about pattern interrupts, and it’s the solution to breaking subconscious patterns that produce bad results.

The idea goes that once you can see a destructive pattern you can break it. For example, if someone has a stutter and they want to get rid of it, then every time they find themselves about to stutter, they can take a radically different action to break the pattern. Here’s how I used the technique…

Years ago I was petrified of public speaking. I spent several years going to Toastmasters to face my fear. I thought I had got good. Then my bank boss asked me to deliver a speech to a room full of 2000 bankers.

The audience would be made up of every leader I’d ever worked with. And every possible leader I might want to work with in the future. To top it off, days before, I’d found out I was going to lose my job because my team was being disbanded.

5 years of work down the drain.

These high stakes changed the game. Before, I was giving speeches to strangers so it was easier. But this audience felt like one mistake could get me fired and make me unemployed forever.

Right before the speech I nearly poo’d my pants. No joke. My hands were sweaty, I felt like I was going to faint, and I worried wee would gush out while I was on stage.

30 seconds before the speech, I had a panic attack.

I couldn’t do it.

That’s when I had to pull out the only tool I had left: a pattern interrupt. I walked up on stage in a panic. I looked for something to interrupt the pattern.

I saw a big, gold bell. Without hesitation I grabbed the bell and rang it so damn loudly the audience thought I’d lost my mind.

I started giggling like a school girl.

The audience smiled. That bell incident broke my pattern of panic and allowed me to chill out. I gave the speech of my life and got a standing ovation at the end.

In that moment the flow state and stream of consciousness was so strong, I felt superhuman. I went from panic to thought leader on a dime all because of a silly pattern interrupt.

Use pattern interrupts to break unconscious patterns.

How you quietly build the skill of pattern recognition

Nobody’s born with patterns pre-installed in their brain.

You can only recognize what you’ve seen before, which means the entire game is loading your brain with the right reps that let you see the right patterns. Here’s how.

1. Do extreme numbers of reps

You cannot recognize a pattern you’ve never encountered. Period.

The person who’s seen 1,000 sales calls reads a prospect in seconds. The amateur is guessing. So you need reps, and a lot of them.

But not passive reps.

Watching the same show for 20 years won’t do what Michael Larson did in a few weeks. Because he wasn’t watching. He was studying.

2. Chase feedback like your life depends on it.

This is the one everybody skips.

Experience only compounds into skill when you find out whether you were right or wrong. Michael Larson paused the VCR frame by frame.

That’s a brutally tight feedback loop.

Guess the pattern, check the tape, correct, repeat. Without feedback, “20 years of experience” is just one year lived 20 times. With it, a few months can beat a career.

3. Get close to the raw data.

Patterns live in the reps themselves, not in summaries of the reps.

Read the actual contracts, not the takeaways. Watch the actual game film, not the highlights. Look at the raw thing everyone else is too lazy or too important to look at. That’s where the structure is hiding.

4. Name your patterns and collect them like a psychopath.

The moment you can name a pattern, you own it.

High performers are secretly dirty little hoarders. They collect mental models, recurring setups, “oh, this is one of those situations” moments, and file them away.

Every time you catch a pattern, name it and add it to the shelf. Your library grows. Your glance gets faster.

5. Study across fields, not just your own.

The deepest patterns repeat everywhere.

The same shape shows up in biology, markets, relationships, and history but looks different each time.

The more domains you collect from, the more often you’ll walk into a “new” problem and think, “Wait, I’ve seen this before.” You haven’t. Not exactly. But your brain found the matching shape. That’s the superpower.

I once met a guy running a university. He was studying airlines like a madman. He took strategies from air travel and applied them to university. He became known as a crazy innovator. But he told me he wasn’t innovating at all.

He was just remixing together two industries that hadn’t been remixed before to produce outlier outcomes. Smart. Do that. Get naughty. Get weird.

6. Study history like a scholar with high pants and nerd glasses smoking a pipe

The best patterns lie in history.

Why? Because history doesn’t repeat but it rhymes. Most people are not looking for solutions from stuff that happened 500 years ago. So, if you do, you’ll look new and innovative. Ryan Holiday did this with stoicism.

He took philosophy from the Romans, that most people weren’t focusing on, and made it valuable and relevant for millennials and teeny boppers like me.

When you study history, you’ll see the most transformative patterns such as:

  • Money doesn’t go to the smartest. It goes to the most resourceful.

  • Governments don’t solve problems. They create them.

  • Poverty in some parts of the world will never die

  • Politicians benefit themselves, not you

  • There will always be war

Study history if you want to predict the patterns of the future. Human nature is so predictable and obvious, it’s scary.

Seeing patterns is not enough. You need this skill.

I’ve gotta let you down again because I am not your guru.

Pattern recognition isn’t enough. And it’s not the highest form of intelligence either. Sorry. Please don’t tell my mommy.

The highest form of intelligence is:

Pattern Recognition + Synthesis

One without the other only leads to stupidity and being fake-smart with a PhD. You must be able to see patterns and connect topics coherently.

This is how you create new ways of solving problems. As I’ve already proven, everyone can see patterns if they want to (many people refuse though).

But few people connect the patterns.

This is why I love writing online. Writing is just thinking. When you write about topics you see patterns and subconsciously join the dots as you write. I don’t even realize I’m doing it half the time. It’s a superpower.

The brutal truth

You either see patterns, or subconscious patterns run your life and make you a slave to circumstances and fate. There is no alternative. That’s gonna piss a lot of people off but so be it.

Pattern recognition is nothing new.

The most successful people in history have been studying patterns and joining the dots between them for centuries. They just rarely talk about it.

So consuming more information, listening to gurus, or spending 10,000 hours playing the violin to a bedroom audience of your cat and dog isn’t going to make you successful.

The brutal truth is patterns run the world. And those who consciously choose to see the patterns, join the dots, and use pattern interrupts when bad patterns take over… are the people who are guaranteed to win.

Everyone else will be controlled by hidden patterns spread by algorithmic newsfeeds that keep them stuck in an echo chamber of their own awesomeness and “I’m right and you’re wrong.”

The future belongs to pattern recognizers. Master pattern recognition.

P.S.

Ok here’s a bonus.

I’ve recognized a main pattern coaching people starting or scaling digital businesses:

There is an obvious business model to make 6 figures.

Cool huh?

The problem is, some business models are doomed to be trapped in 4-figure or 5-figure hell.

Right model, great business.

Wrong model, struggling business.
