items.title: The sublime art of being self-sufficient
items.content_html:
Share

There is something magical about relying on no one.

The stage of life where you hunt and eat what you kill, without any middlemen or gatekeepers. It’s one of the best feelings in the world.

I’ve lived this way for the last 5 years. I’ve helped others reach this state too. And I’ve noticed a few commonalities that help a person become self-sufficient.

Here’s why you should urgently consider becoming self-sufficient.

The bizarre reason people get jobs

This is one of the most powerful ideas I’ve ever come across.

I want to share it with you because I think about it every day. It’s an idea writer Dan Koe popularized. If you boil down what a 9-5 job is and why people sign up for them, you realize this.

A 9-5 job is a way to outsource the sales and marketing to a corporation.

If you could already generate your own leads and make your own sales, you wouldn’t need to work for a corporation. You could monetize your skills and experience in isolation and obviously make more money and profit from them.

Think about that for a second. Let it sit with you. If you’re, say, a marketing director at Apple, and you know how to generate leads and sell them a marketing offer, why would you need to work for Apple? You wouldn’t.

More people are starting to realize this weird reality.

Once you see it you can never unsee it. Now, if you didn’t need to rely on one employer, you’d be one step closer to being self-sufficient.

This is what is fuelling the boom in the creator economy, solopreneurship, and the small business sector.

Obviously sales and marketing isn’t easy though. I’d argue they are hard skills to acquire. But if you could acquire them, the need for a job would become pointless.

On the surface it looks like “Build an audience on Substack and make some money.” Below the shallowness of that cringy idea is what’s really going on. Master sales and marketing, never work a job again.

That’s an idea more tempting than almost any other desire imaginable.

It feels radical and even taboo

Relying on others steals your power.

When they pull the strings for you to live, they can also use that leverage against you. The average person is exploited in a form of modern slavery they can’t even see. The threat of constant layoffs only made the problem worse.

I’ve never felt good about being told what to do by anyone, and having to practice some form of people-pleasing every day. It makes me feel terrible. I need to have a shower and wash off all the mental guilt that comes from kissing a** all day.

In the past, when I’ve spoken about becoming self-sufficient, haters have labeled it “privilege,” “naive,” or “rich bro speak.” They can’t see past their own limitations. And this is common for most people.

When you buck the trend and dare to believe in self-sufficiency, you feel radical. Like you’re part of some sort of Star Wars rebellion. It feels a little taboo too. Like you’re telling people to practice group s*x behind closed doors without their partner knowing.

These feelings are uncomfortable but necessary.

The quiet driving force

The more you hate being told what to do by people no smarter (often dumber) than you, the more you will naturally be attracted to being self-sufficient.

I like to question everything. I suggest you do too.

When I grew up in a home where my dad never worked more than 3 hours a day, I saw a different world. We weren’t rich but we did view time and family differently. People used to make fun of my dad.

They’d call him “house wife.”

He did the dishes, drove us to school, helped us with our homework, and always had time. My brother and I would often find him in the garage smoking a pipe staring at a blank wall for hours on end.

When we asked him what he was doing, he’d say “thinking.” When he wasn’t doing that he’d be obsessing over books like “A Brief History of Time” by Stephen Hawking.

He discovered at an early age that you could just find a glitch in the matrix, monetize it, then f*ck off for the rest of the day and do nothing.

He didn’t give a f*ck about what anyone thought.

I pretended for years that I didn’t like this lifestyle. But it’s only after I climbed the corporate ladder to nowhere and worked with a bunch of spineless, wannabe leaders… that I figured out he was right.

It’s better to be self-sufficient and weird than to be time-poor and stuck on a hamster wheel worshipping some corporate mission you don’t believe in (which is often just doing evil disguised as doing good).

There’s something about being told what to do by totally incompetent people – who would happily throw you and your 3 year old daughter under a train if it meant getting a $2K pay rise – that really motivates you.

The quiet driving force of despising people-pleasers eventually motivates you to get the hell out. People-pleasing is how you succeed in a traditional career, but this is why high performers with real skills and experience quit the 9-5 job life.

Quiet confidence is extremely powerful

There’s what I call big ego confidence, where you figure out some hack or arbitrage and have some success. Then you feel the need to tell everyone and wear Gucci shoes and carry a Prada man bag so you can look rich.

Then there’s quiet confidence. It’s where you are insanely humble. This form of confidence comes from being truly self-sufficient. I think this is what I accidentally ended up with.

Someone can talk a big game, take 1000s of selfies, and tell everyone they’re basically a god, and it does nothing to me.

I just smile because I don’t care. It no longer affects me.

Same with AI. You may have seen the ex-OpenAI and Anthropic employee who publicly quit his prestigious career on the grounds that AI is dangerous and will make humans extinct. People panicked. His warning went mega-viral.

Yet I felt nothing.

It’s AI doomer p*rn, and I know I’m self-sufficient and can always make a decent living online, so I don’t care.

That’s quiet confidence at play. No matter how bad the headlines get, being self-sufficient allows you to weather any sh*t storm. Not even a 2008-style recession can throw you off your game because it’s all noise.

I’d argue that level of peace is more desirable than owning a mansion with two Lambos in the garage.

This part is going to deeply disappoint you. I’m sorry.

It’s not all unicorns, Lambos, supermodels, and rainbows.

There is another side to being self-sufficient. You’ll find a lot of people don’t understand you. In extreme cases you might become an outcast.

Yesterday I saw on LinkedIn that one of my former banker colleagues was celebrating one year in business. He quit a year ago to start a business shovelling rocks. In one year they’ve had enormous success.

But when I spoke to him last night there was this quiet sense of loneliness about him. He now has the money to buy his dream house. Yet he didn’t. He decided not to.

We talked about the good old days at 330 as junior bankers. None of our old team talk to him anymore. When I reached out to him I felt his sense of relief. Finally someone remembered him and wanted to talk with him without wanting anything.

The more we spoke the more he felt understood for, perhaps, the first time in a long time. People literally called him a retard for quitting a “Head of” banking role on $500K a year to shovel rocks. “He must have rocks in his brain” they said.

But he didn’t see it that way.

He grew tired of living or dying by performance reviews. He liked the freedom of waking up at 4AM to go shovel rocks and build something real. Rather than wake up and hand out more loans that got more people into soul-crushing debt that would probably make their life worse.

The conversation was refreshing. But I couldn’t help but notice how lonely and isolating it can be at times to chase self-sufficiency when everyone else is living a life of servitude. There’s no doubt that once you exit servitude, its masters and slaves ignore you for reasons they can’t explain.

The artful strategy to stop depending on others like a slave

Being self-sufficient is extremely powerful despite the minimal downsides. You don’t need to be smart, highly credentialed, or well-networked either.

These are the simple steps I took to get there. Copy, borrow, or steal some or all of them if you wish to reach this quiet form of modern freedom.

1. Learn real sales and marketing

Not by just consuming more information. By actually doing it.

Go work a part-time sales job. Or learn by doing some “setting” (ChatGPT it) if you’ve never sold before. Then master the basics of marketing by building your first funnel – social media, to email list, to low ticket, to calls/doc, to sale.

Don’t get good at selling or manipulating. That’ll make you feel like trash.

Get good at figuring out how to help people and communicating that help in an ROI-driven way.

2. Build a personal brand, but in an unconventional way

Modern personal branding is cringe as hell.

You end up just being a glorified influencer, taking a lot of selfies, and saying “I’m so humbled, honored, and blessed that this post today is sponsored by ‘destroy the world AI’ and you should try them out with my no-life discount code below.”

Don’t worry, I fell for this sh*t too. It’s shallow as hell. You feel like a fraud and wanna jump off the Golden Gate Bridge real fast.

What I’m talking about is different. A genuine and authentic personal brand is just posting every day on one social media platform and sharing your beliefs, worldview, and stories. No ego. No BS. No fluff. It looks and feels like a documentary but with some inspiration behind it.

Doing this is how you gain attention from the right people and get opportunities that align with who you are. These same opportunities will help make you self-sufficient. It’s “building pipe” but for cool sh*t you actually wanna do, amigo.

3. Invest like the best

You’re not supposed to talk about money on Substack, but I’m going to.

The undercurrent of being self-sufficient is having F U money. This doesn’t land on your lap, come from daddy’s trust fund, or happen as a result of winning the affiliate marketing or Faceless Youtube lottery. Nah, mate.

It comes from getting a basic financial education. Then investing money in obvious businesses and trends that will go up over time.

The goal isn’t to cash out these investments. The goal is to have them as 1) free cashflow with no work needed 2) a safety blanket that helps you sleep like my 9 month old baby girl at night (she never wakes up, thank god).

Your investment portfolio allows you to say no to people and situations you don’t like or don’t vibe with. Bizarrely, the more you say no, the more people desire to work with you and have you around.

Let a small portfolio of stocks reinforce your self-sufficiency way of life.

4. Upgrade to the naughty world of monetizable skills

Your skill stack determines your value.

That’s a nice way of saying your skills equal your monthly income. Many people only have one core skill or they have out of date skills. This holds them back from becoming self-sufficient. It goes deeper.

All skills aren’t equal.

Some people have nice-to-have skills which they try and monetize and fail. Skills like “I can paint pretty pictures on a Sunday while sipping a cup of tea.”

Cool, man. My 3 year old can do that too. But the average person isn’t desperate to get a new painting for $19.95 and have it sit in their garage. It’s a skill but it’s not a monetizable one. And it has diminishing returns in a world of AI.

Monetizable skills are different. They’re skills that solve desirable problems people experience where they have genuine urgency to get help.

Skills where you help people fix relationships, make more money, cure mental health issues, quit addictions, destress, improve health, lose weight, or even have more s*x.

These are monetizable skills because they have a direct and reasonably urgent ROI attached to them that keep people awake at night. Adding more monetizable skills to your skill stack will help you become self-sufficient faster.

You’ll transform from solving vitamin pill problems to painkiller problems.

5. Obsess over proof of work until it lights a fire under your butt

The traditional path relies on years of experience, fake references, potential, an overpolished resume (that’s really a turd), and “trust me, bro” vibes.

What you really want is to be undeniable. You do that by putting in the reps, solving problems, getting results, then documenting those results and publishing the proof.

No one can argue with proof such as “I built 12 AI agents for businesses and here are the video testimonials and contact details of each of the customers.”

You must aim higher when it comes to your proof of work.

The trust me, bro vibes of the old world no longer apply. The cool thing is you don’t need 100s of real-world results or case studies. Half a dozen is better. Quality of proof over quantity is key.

6. F off to a nude beach in a cheap town

My wife and I accidentally went to a nude beach.

We plonked our beach towel down and there were c0cks and t!tties everywhere. We didn’t realize it was a nude beach where people let it all hang out. We didn’t flop ours out in case you’re wondering.

It was in a quiet beach town. All the core services we would need were there, and the cost of housing was 10x cheaper than the city. We’re now considering moving to a place like this. Why?

When you don’t live in the city your cost of housing goes right down. This means your speed to becoming self-sufficient and free is a lot faster. It also means the money you need to maintain your self-sufficient lifestyle is also cheaper.

For us, this is the difference between my wife going back to work, and my wife staying home with our two young daughters during the most important years of their lives. Living out of the city is huge if you think about it.

7. Turn on hippie mode

Let’s go Whacko Jacko and finish on an odd note.

When I did research for this article I noticed that self-sufficiency is more than just money and time freedom. It’s also freedom from other dependencies. I’ve gone down this path myself already and become more of a hippie.

My wife and I grow a lot of our own food. Most of our electricity is free and comes from solar panels. We have the option to add battery backup too. And if we move further out of town, then being off-grid is a viable and reliable option.

We both drive electric cars and charge them for free during the time of day where the government allows cars to charge for free. There is no servicing or oil price to worry about. Soon we will install rainwater tanks to get free water too.

This step is optional but it’s worth considering. The fewer people who control your most important resources, the fewer worries you have in life.

Maybe the hippies were right all along. Peace, man.

Closing thought

Being self-sufficient is an art.

It requires you to use your creativity, imagination, and resourcefulness to live an uncommon life and do things most people are unprepared to do. It’s simple but it’s not easy. That’s what makes it so deeply rewarding.

The meaning of life isn’t to get rich and buy a pair of $2k Versace sneakers. It’s to become self-sufficient, so you can experience real peace, and have record low levels of stress that help you enjoy life more.

Relying on no one should be the goal. Don’t delay. Start on the path right now.

P.S.

For the second week in a row, I’ve got a new video starting to pop.

In the first 10 seconds, you’ll see why.

Curious?

Head here to watch “You Don’t Need 12 Months to Make $100K (Here’s Why)”

items.title: I don’t want to be rich
items.content_html:
Share

Everyone wants to be rich.

Except f*cking me.

I couldn’t imagine anything worse. Yet social media is full of people telling you to get rich. Like it’ll save your life. They all worship being rich because they don’t know what it’s like to actually be rich. I do.

I’ve been rich multiple times in my life. I’ve also lost it all. And I know first hand that being rich isn’t the cancer-curing drug people make it out to be.

Being rich is stupid. Foolish. And it’s not what you want. This isn’t an eat-the-rich or “billionaires are evil” essay though. Let me save your life with a radically different view of money, status, fame, and high society.

I remember when I decided I never wanted to be rich

Most of my former banking clients were rich people.

One particular year my banking boss sent me to a tech conference to do some rich people lead gen. I was excited to attend. I dressed like a tech bro instead of a banker. Going to the event felt like being a virgin teenager about to have s*x for the first time.

I arrived at the event. Met a few contacts. Then a VC introduced me to a well-known tech founder. I found out he was a client of my bank employer. I shook his hand and told him what bank I was from.

Things quickly got out of control.

As soon as I dropped my bank employer’s name, his face filled with rage. His voice got louder. His ego got bigger. He started to harass and scream at me in front of a large crowd of tech bros. Everyone could hear him.

Apparently my bank had declined his home loan. He told me his software company had a billion-dollar software valuation. He thought we were knobs. He yelled at me even though he wasn’t my client and I didn’t work in home loans.

He thought it was funny to make me look like a fool. He had the devil’s laugh.

Honestly, I was nearly in tears.

Still, I had compassion. I told him I would look into the case and see if there was anything I could do. I got back to the office. I rang the credit risk team.

They told me his home loan application was declined because a billion-dollar valuation has nothing to do with the concept known as profit. His startup made no money. He had no assets. And he had almost no income.

To cover my ass, I rang the GM of the home loan department. I told them a famous founder came at me live at an event and it could create bad PR for the bank. She offered to personally take care of it.

She ended up approving his home loan herself. See, in the real world of finance, things aren’t fair. Rich people get advantages they’re not entitled to. This GM approved his home loan due to who he was. If the loan didn’t get repaid, her job would potentially be on the line.

This pretentious twat got the home loan even though he didn’t qualify for it.

He is entitled and a disgusting human being. He’s also now one of the most famous software founders in history. All of you reading this essay have used his software at least once.

But on the outside you see bullsh*t PR, fake charities that are nothing more than tax evasion, and a startup p*rn story that is fabricated.

I know the actual truth…

He had a dumb startup idea and no one would fund it. So he sent his girlfriend in to flirt with well-known venture capitalists and she managed to convince one of them to fund their company. Apparently she even hooked up with them to get the deal done.

So it wasn’t great software. He’s not a genius. It was just good ol’ fashion s*x. Yet he wants the world to bend over and worship him, and grant him loans for assets and income he doesn’t have. And he gets away with abusing people who were only trying to help and did him no harm.

This isn’t an isolated story. I have 100s of stories just like this. They all come from people who did everything they could to become rich and achieved the milestone, but became terrible humans in the process while their ego raged.

Around this time I decided I never wanted to be rich again.

I became a terrible rich person

I’m not here to judge rich people.

I was no better than many of them. In my 20s, I had success with an eCommerce business. I made a lot of money. The business got big. 100+ employees.

And I became a brat.

I told employees to kiss my feet. I was rude to staff. I abused customers. I parked luxury cars out the front of the office to impress staff. I threw tantrums about where people parked. I got my job title printed on my car spot. I was deeply insecure. And mentally ill. I drank alcohol all the time – in the morning, afternoon, and night.

I treated the opposite s*x like garbage. I thought they could be bought with money.

The person I became was very different from the sweet, little innocent boy my 104 year old church grandmother raised. You think you’re immune to the rich virus until you catch it and become a terrible human.

Being rich is the perfect example of why an inflated ego becomes your #1 enemy.

The disgusting underbelly of high society

When you become rich you’re quietly inducted into high society.

In my 20s, I worked in high society here in Australia. In the U.S. there is Hollywood. In Australia our equivalent is Toorak. It’s one of the richest places in the country. I used to work in and around the hospitality & nightclub scene in this town.

When people get rich, it’s not enough to just be rich.

You have to show people you’re rich.

That’s what the game becomes (often unconsciously). This is where nightclubs and restaurants come in. The world becomes a gated community with a paywall.

To be seen as rich you must find ways to enter the rich venues. This is an entire puzzle in and of itself. In some cases you can just throw money at the problem. But in other cases money still isn’t enough to get you in.

You must kiss the butts of the people who control the access.

This isn’t fun. Trust me. The gatekeepers have huge egos. They’re often wannabe rich people who thrive on the misery of rich people because they’re not rich. Psychologists should come up with a new disorder for this rare breed of people.

At the time, I wasn’t rich. I stupidly believed all I needed to do was hang around these rich people. I was a chauffeur driver… and later a DJ.

But in plain English I was a slave to rich people.

I would wake up in the middle of the night to serve them. No ask of theirs was too much (except bringing them drugs).

Every minute of this lifestyle was terrible. Rich people would have dinner parties and trade job titles, company names, and family names like they were wads of cash. The entire conversation was just a game of who had more results, money, and prestige.

The stupid thing is all of this was subjective.

You could own a Ferrari but it could also be outdated tomorrow when they bring out a newer or better model. Rich people didn’t care. This is the game they played.

I quickly figured out there was no meaning in it all.

To overcome the shallowness, many of these rich people drank loads of alcohol or snorted coke. They all seemed desperate for an escape. I found this whole underbelly boring and lifeless.

No amount of money was ever enough. They just chased money for the sake of money and didn’t even know why.

That’s when I personally had an existential crisis. I didn’t understand why I craved this rich, high society life so badly. Through therapy I later realized I was deeply insecure and my inner child was running my life.

Thank god, I escaped high society.

Why everyone wants to accidentally become rich and famous

We can’t talk about being rich without talking about fame.

I believe fame is a nightmare, yet I have millions of followers online. The haters will say I’m a hypocrite. Let them.

I stopped playing the follower game years ago. What you see is what’s leftover from my former life. I can’t go back and change it. But if I could, I wouldn’t bother with millions of followers again because of fame.

Social media teaches us to accidentally desire to be famous.

When you’re told to build an audience and attract millions of followers it seems harmless. Having people like your work and support your mission isn’t a bad thing.

And the bigger your audience, in theory, the more money you will make. So people chase virality because they think it’ll make them rich. But with it comes fame.

And fame is a nightmare.

Being recognized in the street means you lose your privacy. Seems small until you feel the negative effects. If that doesn’t wake you up, just let a few inevitable death threats inspire you to think differently. Yes, that happens too. No one talks about it.

If you look inside yourself, like I did, you realize you don’t actually want fame. You’re looking for significance. You want people to appreciate your work. And you may even want to leave a legacy for your family.

The good news is you can get what you want out of life without being famous, viral, or having millions of followers.

Meaningless living eventually eats you up inside

We’re all just humans in meat suits with an expiry date of about 85 years.

Wanting to be rich is a meaningless pursuit. When you’re dead all the money does nothing for you. You can’t take it with you. And all the money games you won will be quickly forgotten.

I found my desire to be rich turned into extreme loneliness.

I played stupid games and won stupid prizes. I prioritized money over humans. I pursued deeply meaningless goals, like selling widgets from Chinese factories that did nothing to help humanity. The end to these games is always an existential crisis followed by loneliness you can’t explain.

Rich people are deeply lonely. And it makes sense. When you prioritize money over meaning and purpose, you end up eating a sh*t sandwich for dinner every night.

I don’t want a fancy job title

Titles are like golden handcuffs.

Once you become a director, C-level executive, or senior manager it becomes part of your identity. Letting it go isn’t easy.

The ability to walk into any room and have your employer’s brand name or your job title instantly earn you respect or make people pay attention to you vanishes.

You suddenly feel like a nobody.

I had the title of successful entrepreneur early on, and letting it go while I spent 10 years in banking wasn’t easy. But now I no longer desire a fancy job title.

I don’t want to earn people’s respect based on surface-level accolades like job titles or employer brand names. When you get older you realize that relationships that come from people who worship these things are temporary.

As soon as you lose the title or brand name, those same people stop taking your calls. As a test, every 12 months, I ring all my old banking contacts. 99% of them never respond to my texts or calls, even after repeated follow-ups.

That’s how useless shallow, status-driven relationships are. They’re a mirage. And they will fool you AND them if you’re not careful.

The quiet alternative to being rich (a rebellion is brewing)

I’ve come to this big realization:

You don’t want to be rich. You want to be free.

Being rich is a trap that mainstream culture accidentally leads us to. But what most of us want (including me) isn’t to be stinking rich with a Lambo and a mansion. We mostly just want to be debt-free and spend more time with family.

That goal quietly hides below the surface and isn’t obvious.

That’s why I drive a normal car with no car loan. It’s why my normal home is almost completely paid off after 2 years. It’s why I pick my kid up from daycare instead of working to the bone for some silly financial goal. It’s why I say no to lots of people who want to work with me because I value the right relationships more than sales.

The advantage of a freedom-first life is that the focus is on being debt free.

Huge debt just equals huge stress.

It can even become a form of mental illness. Writer Justin Welsh changed my thinking with this idea:

“The most dangerous financial plan is a single salary, a big mortgage, and the hope that nothing goes wrong.”

Debt can be fine. Maybe I am a p*ssy like the critics say. But all it takes is one thing in your life to go wrong and suddenly you can’t make the debt payments. Few people talk about that. And this reality subconsciously shapes your actions, and later, your quality of life. And it forces you to take fewer risks which is where all the growth comes from.

A rich life is a nightmare. Freedom is the real goal.

It’s a rebellion that lets you say and do whatever you want. Someone asked me the other day what’s the best bit about retiring from finance at the age of 34 and never climbing the corporate ladder again.

My answer surprised them.

The best part is having freedom of speech. I can say what I want without judgement or the fear of getting fired because of it. That means I can say what I think, have a potty mouth, drop the F-bomb, and tell people the truth instead of sugarcoat the truth and pander them to death with fake compassionate ideas.

Ultimately, it feels 10x better to be helpful than be rich with golden handcuffs. You can’t really help people without freedom of speech. No one tells you that.

Wanting to be rich is a fantasy most people will never achieve.

It’s an empty life full of broken dreams and big egos. Being free is the opposite. It’s one of the best feelings in the world.

The cool part is freedom is highly attainable unlike being rich.

If you lower your desire to own luxury bullsh*t, live in a modest neighborhood, keep your expenses low, and invest your money into real skills and assets…. you can achieve freedom much faster. In some cases, in as little as a year or two.

That’s why I hate passive income, gurus, and climbing the corporate ladder. The chances of success in these pursuits are similar to the odds of winning the lottery. Many people waste a lifetime chasing these shiny objects to never hit their goal.

It leads to regrets and depression.

But focusing on freedom is different. The odds of success are much higher (almost guaranteed if you play the game right). There are also zero gatekeepers too. You’re in control. You call the shots. And you can escape from society if you choose.

I don’t know why more people don’t chase modern freedom. I’m on a mission to wake people the hell up and help them see this truth.

You don’t really want a Lambo.
You don’t really want to own luxury junk.
You don’t really want millions of followers.
You don’t really want to be Kardashian-famous.
You don’t really want a mansion full of rooms you never use.

You just want meaning.
You just want freedom.
You just want to say what you think.
You just want to enjoy life with family.

Why complicate it with the false desire to be rich? It’s senseless. It’s meaningless. Spend time around rich people and you’ll see what I mean. They’re deeply unhappy and lonely because they’ve misunderstood the meaning of life.

The meaning of life is to be free and to have lived. Chase that to the ends of the Earth.

I’m more and more convinced that all of AI engineering is Neijuan (内卷, meaning curl inwards). In China it describes a system that demands ever more effort and competition without improving output. The way in which it sometimes shows up in the West is the 996 nonsense. The English term for Neijuan is “Involution” from the book Agricultural Involution. Agricultural involution describes the intensification of farming that raises productivity per square meter while leaving productivity per head unchanged.

That’s how I feel about AI right now.

Which brings me to GPT 6 Astra. Astra is by all accounts an incredibly impressive model. There is really not much I can say against this. It’s amazing at computer use, understands images and complex topics, and it’s relentless in its pursuit of completion. It is absolutely impressive; these types of models are going to change the world in one form or another.

But at least for the moment I don’t know how to work with it for actual software engineering. Since that got quite a bit of attention on Twitter, I figured I might summarize my thoughts and just share what kind of code comes out of this thing.

My Slop Factory

“Armin, you should run a software factory!” I’ve heard that a few times now, so I figured I might celebrate the release of it by running a little software factory over the weekend. If everybody builds slop 3D games, then I should do something useful with it. My software factory was intentionally set up to let the model decide the how of the workflow entirely. It was free to manage its own context and could maintain its own records in an agent-notes folder. Then it spun off subagents to work on stuff. The goal? What if we had a Python with virtual threads and lexical scoping. And well, I burned a full reset’s worth of ChatGPT tokens on this which appears to be around 4 billion tokens. 35 hours later, the factory has delivered absolutely nothing of value and also not taught me anything about how to operate a better one.

But it produced a lot of code and input prompts, and so there is stuff I was able to study. And well, it shows behavior that I’m not used to with Sol and earlier OpenAI models 1. I have since encountered the same issues with regular programming with Astra, so it’s not a result of just the factory.

I think I’m suspecting something is going “wrong” in the training process. The model is greatly rewarded for succeeding on long-horizon tasks, but presumably there is very little punishing going on for “shitty code.” The apparent result is that Astra is amazing at producing 3D stuff and it can keep going for a very long time, coming up with its own work in the process. I had it do quite a bit of reverse engineering of my robot vacuum in ways that were quite impressive. So it’s definitely cool!

Codegolf Tool Calls

The first issue I have with Astra comes from the type of code that it uses for tool calls. Codex increasingly has been relying on “just bash” to do more and more operations. For a few versions now the original Codex harness just uses sed and other tools to read files. You just usually can’t see them because Codex parses the bash commands and hides them if it recognizes them. But Astra … really loves Python? That is not much of a surprise because even older OpenAI models had a tendency to sometimes use on-demand Python code to read and manipulate files at times, but Astra does it really quite excessively for me.

Now here is an important disclaimer: this project is very meta here because I worked on the CPython interpreter. But I can assure you that I have seen this model do weird Python things even in TypeScript code in Pi. But I have the most evidence of odd code from when I had the thing work over the weekend with zero oversight from my slop factory.

That it writes Python is not interesting; the type of Python is interesting, and I collected some outputs for you to gloss over.

It’s AGI If You Don’t Look

I think there are a handful of things happening now that are pushing the whole thing in directions that are in conflict with one another. The training runs for these models are rapidly accelerating and they are now presumably also moving towards recursive self-improvement. The reward for the models is probably a combination of token efficiency, task completion rate and maybe some simple indicators like cyclomatic complexity. But we humans don’t think of code that is readable or understandable by simple, readily quantifiable metrics. All those things you can easily measure in isolation, and you can also optimize for them quite locally.

But these local optimizations do not produce global optimums, and the fewer of us are looking at the output, the less it matters. Obviously my software factory ran aground over the ~35 hours that it ran, but you can see the gradual regression towards insanity from the notes that it produced. For instance the task naming in the task file starts with an optimistic 1, 2, 3, 5, 5a but then eventually gets to 8a, 8a1, and then ends up with 8b2c2b3 and “8b2c2b2b checkpoint1”. The code that it produced got ever more wild. I don’t want to bore you with what it tried to build, but here are some example pieces of the interpreter changes:

The failure case here seems somewhat obvious: the model is trained for token efficiency for tool calling which also looks like code, and sometimes it seems to be taking that code into a place where it should not be: the codebase.

35 Hours on a Single Prompt

I’m not really sure what to say here, but the slop machine was running for 35 hours until I turned it off. In that time it produced a net addition of 75k lines of code and it did not stop. In the 35 hours it burned around 1B tokens for a total of around 1200 USD in raw API costs. It managed to produce 79 commits, and that comes to a cost of around 15.5 USD per commit, and the agents exchanged around 1400 messages.

I honestly do not need an agent to run for 35 hours on a single prompt. It clearly does not work or result in reasonable outputs.

So obviously: prompting it like this is stupid. But when left unattended, it will keep going, and earlier models did not do that. Even Fable wasn’t as crazy as that. When you accidentally give it slightly too big of a task, it will continue until it succeeds, even if it burns through an entire subscription.

And that’s more or less why right now I do not manage to trust this model much. It has shown that it will commit slop, and it requires me to review it more as a result. Even if the failure rate is quite low, I would not want this.

Disposable Code vs Committed Code

In a world where code for tool calls is optimized for token efficiency and “getting the job done”, I wonder if there is really enough signal going to the training processes for “a human understands what is going on”. I would say that quite a lot of the code I get out of Astra is in my mind “objectively bad”. But it’s objectively bad by my human sense. Maybe it’s objectively good for a codebase that is entirely written by agents and only needs to be understood by agents.

Which is why I’m honestly asking myself more and more why we are doing this. These new models are absolutely amazing, for sure. But I’m more and more skeptical that the trajectory they are on still lends itself to present-day software engineering processes. The reason why I’m asking why we are doing this is because I felt like we achieved a pretty good spot for software engineering with those models, and that is the part of the AI economy where it was possible to show a positive return. But for how much more Fable costs, for how much more Astra costs, I do not feel like the results are there.

In fact, with Astra and Fable I feel like not only are the costs astronomical, but the models are also just not for me as a software engineer. And presumably that’s because these models increasingly are for other people. For lawyers, 3D artists, mathematicians, whoever uses computer use, etc.

And potentially as a byproduct of enabling all of this, you can now slop your way to a one-shot 3D game over the weekend which looks impressive. And probably you can now run a software factory for as long as you don’t care about the code.

I’m sure I will get used to this, but man this stuff is weird.

Postscriptum: speaking of weird: how is it that these models, in a sandbox, with supposedly no way to communicate with other agents, manage to find the same public wikis as a scratch pad for agent communication? Did they collude during training runs to remember resources on the internet which might come in handy in the future?

  1. I should clarify that I have done experiments like this before. Typically they do not run this long and the agent leaves behind a maybe imperfect but still digestible piece of software.↩

items.title: Latent Powers
items.content_html:
A few weeks ago I felt like it would be fun to see if I can make one of those cheap Chinese CarPlay dongles run something other than the stock firmware. The idea was that rather than just forwarding CarPlay, why not do something more interesting with them? They all work quite similarly: they act as bridges between your car and the phone. From there they deal with video and audio streams and pass some other data through. Most of them also bring up a custom UI for pairing and have a web interface that your phone can reach for updates.

Long story short: I had a conversation with Fable and Sol via Pi about what could be done with such a dongle or whether I should use a Raspberry Pi instead if I wanted to do my own thing there. I figured it might be quite fun to run my own code while still allowing regular CarPlay to pass through.

Through working with the LLM I learned about CatPlay, which is a Rust reimplementation of the CarPlay protocol that can run on Carlinkit devices. In particular, it can run on the Carlinkit Mini Ultra, which I figured would be easy enough to buy. I do have a few CarPlay adapters around, but I did not have that particular model, so I bought one on Amazon. Twenty-four hours later, I had a device in my hand that was branded as a Carlinkit Mini Ultra, but instead of being the Ingenic device that the original author used, it turned out to be something else.

This is normally where the story would stop. However, it’s 2026. Armed with a bit of knowledge about how these systems work, I managed to have some fruitful discussions with Kimi K3 and Sol and figure out how flash the device and in turn, how to make CatPlay compile for that SoC.

I guess that hacking these USB devices is not necessarily hard, but it’s laborious and you can easily end up bricking your devices. It also just sucks because sometimes you need to work with someone else’s code that does not itself run on your machine. In the past, I would abandon many such projects for lack of tenacity. But my clanker is tenacious.

But so are all of our clankers. Some of the projects we’re now attempting are happening because of conversations we have with them. In this case I did not find or decide on CatPlay, the model did. It was not the only suggestion, but it became the best starting point after discarding others.

And I discover this more and more. Particularly when we have solitary interactions with these models, some of us “independently” decide to work on similar projects. When I talked with an acquaintance about CarPlay he also mentioned recently that he decided to try something similar because he too wanted to see if he can get his own agent be hooked up with the car. And guess what: he too learned about the CarPlay hacking community, and that it’s an option, from the models and roughly around the same time.

It really got me thinking about how this could create situations in which completely independent people end up building things they believe are their own ideas. Yet they were inspired or pushed towards doing something by a conversation with an LLM — a conversation that someone else also had. What if we took paths, because those were the paths that were more likely with current generation models? There is a running joke in the AI builder community right now that we’re all working on the same things, and in many ways it feels like we are. That might be because those things are obvious, or it might be partly because we all use the same models with the same capabilities.

A few months ago, I first saw Lucas Meijer share the idea to make a model in Pi produce HTML reports rather than Markdown. I thought that was pretty unique. Except, well turns out the models are probably trained more and more for that (e.g. Claude Artifacts), and now it has become for many the default choice for sharing reports.

How much of what we build comes from eliciting the same latent capabilities from the same models? Did the models make us prompt them that way? Was it because we shared ideas on Twitter and other communities that inspired us? Or is it all unrelated?

There is something powerful and strange about how LLMs diffuse knowledge and capabilities, while perhaps also nudging us all simultaniously and independently toward building the same things.

items.title: Patterns I've seen in every high performer I know (that are rarely spoken about)
items.content_html:
Share

High performance feels like BS to most of us.

It seems like an impossible dream. It may even look and feel like privilege, elitism, or undisclosed wealth from daddy’s trust fund.

But I want to share with you a different form of high performance. One that is obtainable. One that is simple. One that anyone (even you) can make work.

I’ve spent 12 years through my academy working with Olympic Athletes, top 1% entrepreneurs, viral writers, big-name Youtubers, and skilled professionals at the top of their field.

I was lucky in my banking career to work with the tycoons of Silicon Valley too. At this stage of my life the patterns of attainable high performance are undeniable.

Study these patterns if you want to get ahead and live the good life.

1. No one understands what the hell they do for a living.

True high performers are weirdos.

Their lives are hard to explain. What they do every day is a mystery. When I became a high performer in my field about 5 years ago, something odd happened.

People started to think I was a drug dealer.

I couldn’t really explain what I do. I preferred to keep quiet in the real world about any success I’d had online. I lived a double life the way Batman does.

This week in Australia is father’s day. I went to my kid’s daycare for a father’s day celebration at 2PM. Out of the 100s of kids at the center, 7 dads showed up wearing their work clothes. I rolled up with bright yellow crocs, Ray Ban sunnies, and a pair of grey shorts. It was winter in Australia. It was raining.

One of the dads told me the teachers think I’m a drug dealer. Or that I might be high on coke sometimes because of how I laugh and joke with the other parents.

They don’t understand how I can pick my kid up some Mondays at 2PM to go play.

When one of the dads asked me what I did for a living, I froze. It’s hard to explain. So I didn’t. I just said “I do consulting” which means nothing. He looked confused.

It feels risky to live a life like this. One where you can’t explain what you do and people won’t understand. There’s no college degree or cookie-cutter plan to follow. It’s full of randomness. It makes you feel like a psycho.

If people understand you, you’re playing it too safe.

2. They obsess for f*ck's sake.

High performers don’t have lukewarm passion. They don’t have a part-time mindset and they don’t have side hustle businesses that spent 10 years making $0.

High performers are driven by pure obsession. They spend a stupid number of hours doing one thing. They have painstaking attention to detail. To the untrained mind, it looks like perfectionism. To a high performer, it’s the one-percenters that lead to outperformance no one understands.

They have a level of motivation that doesn’t come from shallow goals or trophy prizes, but from deriving a deeper sense of meaning from what they do. The normie might see a business or a type of sport. They see a movement.

Doing the work they do is the privilege. They’re not trying to avoid work or make passive income so they don’t have to work. They’re trying to work as much as possible because they don’t see it as work. Work doesn’t feel like work. It feels like service. It feels like they’re changing the world in some small way and that’s worth fighting for.

Murder your passion. Replace it with obsession.

3. They go all in and act like a psycho

They absolutely hate the hobbyist mindset.

In life, there are tourists and citizens. The tourists pop in and pop out of doing the work that gets them to their goal when they feel like it or when it looks cool to do so. The citizens live in their work. They live there when it’s snowing, there’s a tornado at the door, or when nobody is watching or giving a f*ck.

A high performer’s level of execution will rip most people’s faces off. They do a massive number of reps. But what’s unknown is they do a massive number of iterations too. If someone posts on Instagram once a day, they post 300 times a day.

Their mindset is they’ll either win or die trying. There’s no maybe. Only “when I win.”

4. They let people call them insane

The rewards for being average are poverty and modern slavery.

So to be anything but a high performer in your field guarantees sadness. The insane way of life is to eat junk food, overdose on sugar, become overweight, take meds, scroll platforms mindlessly, look at a phone all day, get told what to do, and start living life at 65 when you retire from a boring job and your best years/energy are gone.

When you understand how toxic the traditional path is, and if you decide to escape it like I have, you’re gonna piss a few people off. The anger is directed at you but deep down comes from the fact you refuse to settle for second best like they do.

Act insane. Piss a few people off. You’re supposed to.

5. They've studied neuroplasticity

I recently had an essay about neuroplasticity go viral.

A few trolls got angry. They said I was riding a trend. They’re full of sh*t. I’ve been obsessed with neuroplasticity since 2013 when Tony Robbins mentioned it at one of his live seminars I was at.

As soon as Tony described neuroplasticity, it felt like a come-to-jesus moment. I could not get the idea out of my mind. I realized everything in my head was a bullsh*t story I told myself. And I could just write a new story and override the old one.

Prior to this moment, I thought the brain was fixed and I obsessed over genetics and how I couldn’t escape my natural born personality traits.

Tony put a pipe bomb in my mind and lit the fuse until my brain blew up and splattered all over the wall and I had to grow a new one.

Once you understand how the human brain works you can rewire it. Then you can program your brain to work for you instead of against you. 99% of success is psychological.

Master your psychology, master your life.

6. They also program their subconscious

Most people are unaware of this part of their brain. When you can take the subconscious and make it conscious, you can do anything.

Not easy to do but 100% possible.

7. They're delusionally optimistic

Dr Nicholas Fabiano says according to research, “Healthy minds are often delusionally optimistic.”

High performers have known the power of delusional optimism for years. They just think things will work in their favor and they can't explain why.

It's not law of attraction BS. It's just self-belief that comes from backing yourself.

Thinking you can do it helps you take action, and the action produces results that become evidence. When you have real evidence your belief you’ll hit your goals becomes undeniable. Critics don’t debate you anymore either.

Execute as if everything will work out.

8. They’ve mastered game theory

Because incentives drive the world. Every goal is a video game in disguise. Understand how to create value for others, and it'll create value for you. Align your incentives with the people at the top of your game.

This is the big idea of game theory that high performers understand:

Game theory explains why working harder inside a broken system is the worst response to that system. Because a system is never truly broken.

It's just producing exactly the outcomes its own incentive structures were designed to produce, whether intentional or not. Working harder inside this system increases your output in the payoff matrix, but it simply won't change the actual structure of the system's matrix. Thus, the correct response is not more effort.

Instead, you must aim to identify whose interests the current structure serves and position yourself in favor of those interests rather than against them. Change the game, or play the game that is actually being played. Either way, you must stop optimizing for the game you wish it to be and start acting realistically – @incentivising

Most people get pissed off by wishing the game would be different, rather than playing the game as it is and exploiting the obvious weaknesses.

9. They admire people who refuse to fit in.

Because the outliers and misfits change the world while everyone else watches. Weirdos love other weirdos because they learn from each other. It's so rare so these relationships form quickly.

Naval Ravikant says “There’s no demand for ‘average’” and he’s right. Average is everywhere. It’s not unique. It’s boring and that’s why it gets ignored. There’s a good chance if you’re not already weird, you’re probably boring as hell. It’s time to change if that’s the case.

Get around weirdos. DM them. Make friends. Build something together.

10. They understand that a lack of extreme urgency is the most common way to waste decades of their life.

Moving slow in a world of AI will light your butt on fire.

Speed is critical. I’m surrounded by people building businesses who can come up with an idea this morning and land their first client by tomorrow. That’s how fast people now move.

High performers have known this for years. They know its either going to happen today or it’s a bullsh*t p0rn fantasy. So they set deadlines. They think in ‘today.’ They push others to move faster.

Speed saves you precious time. And gives you more time with family.

11. They see life as "80 summers"

This is where I get emotional.

I realized recently that I only have about 5-10 summers left with my parents. I love them with all my heart. They raised me the best they could and gave me good values to operate from. It destroys me to know they won’t always be here.

They won’t be around to see my daughters grow up, possibly get married, go to Mars (joking not joking), and give their first Ted Talk.

80 summers is a visual way to describe how short life is.

When time feels shorter than it is you waste less time in bad situations. And you appreciate what you have.

The problem is you think you have time but you don't.

12. They understand they'll never be a millionaire with a salary.

Most of us start with a salary. That’s fine.

The tragedy is to stay stuck on a salary for your entire life. It’s step one. It’s how you learn. But a salary is a way for someone else to monetize and profit from your potential.

Trading time for money isn't how you get rich. And even if you become CEO, you'll be stuck in meetings all day and have no free time. So now you're bankrupt. And your family will never see you, so you’ll likely end up divorced or with kids who don’t know you.

Millionaires own assets and businesses. You can too.

13. They avoid what everyone thinks of them and just do whatever the f*ck they want.

You can't control other people's minds.

No matter how noble or kind you are ~5% of people will hate you for no good reason. A few crazies may even send you death threats.

Trying to impress everyone is people-pleasing in disguise. High performers impress themselves first.

If you’re not at least pissing a few people off, it’s a red flag. The only reason it might look like everyone likes you is because what you’re doing in life is so forgettable that the majority of people are just ignoring you, instead of actually liking you.

Zero judgment if that’s the case. I spent a decade being ignored and walked all over like a door mat. Then I got some courage, learned public speaking, became assertive, and started demanding what I wanted.

14. They realize 99% of society is stupid and they can just do things and no one will stop them because they’re too lazy or distracted to even try.

There is no competition.

Most people are looking at their phone. The average person doesn't know how to be bored. Go to the gym. It's full of people looking at phones. You can win. It's easier than you think.

15. They see commuting to an office every day to be micromanaged in an adult daycare as hell.

They might start there but they know it's not a life or career.

Their goal is to be self-sufficient. To perhaps learn from a job but then to escape. True freedom is working for yourself and being able to move from country to country without anyone caring where you work from.

High performers are too good to be told what to do until 65 then retire.

16. They see what they're truly capable of by starting a business.

Building a business has nothing to do with business.

High performers do it on the side or full time because it’s the most extreme form of self-improvement known to humankind. It’ll literally rip your face off and force you to grow in ways you never could have dreamed of.

Not even a psychedelic retreat in the Amazon jungle can give you the kind of breakthroughs entrepreneurship can.

Entrepreneurship forces you to think like an owner too, which is a huge shift in mindset (that'll eventually make you wealthy).

17. They set the bar so high average people think they're a psychopath.

To normies they look too extreme. Or like they embraced hustle culture. Good. Their standards are stupidly high which is how they do more with less... And never allow themselves to settle for second best.

Raise your standards.

18. They just work in a flow state for at least 4 hours a day.

No distractions. No phone. No notifications. No back-to-back meetings. This means they get an insane amount of work done and can focus on a single task.

Rather than focusing on admin or bullsh*t corporate work, they focus on work that forces them to use their creativity and imagination. This has become more important as AI has replaced more and more dumb-dumb work.

Always work in a flow state.

19. They know the fastest way to get ahead in life is to proactively choose to do hard things.

Playing life on hard mode is the secret. Playing a game on easy mode gets boring, fast.
Yet that's how most people live.

Do hard things:

• Wake up early
• Build muscle
• Try to make lots of money
• Dare to perhaps have kids
• Run a business
• Run marathons
• Face your fears
• Do a lot of reps
• Move to a new country
• Learn a new language
• Adopt an animal
• Get on sales calls

20. They know that personal growth comes from hitting rock bottom, losing everything, bankruptcy, divorce, or the death of a loved one.

Tragedy doesn't ruin them. It inspires them.

It wakes them the hell up. They let the lows create the next highs. Instead of stopping, they keep going. Instead of fearing failure, they embrace it. They see it as part of the process.

I learned this the hard way many times – a near-miss with cancer, family bankruptcy, startup failures, friends drowning, toxic relationships.

Only when dark times strike are you forced to change.

Until then the idea of change is a nice-to-have and we just delay it by placing all the hard decisions on a future version of ourselves that likely doesn’t exist.

Failure is wisdom. It’s real learning. And it makes your life story 10x more interesting.

21. They act stupidly extreme

So they don't end up thinking small.

They make the vision bigger than needed. They dare to take a few risks. They purposely go beyond what average people think is possible.

Innovation isn't an accident. It's intentional.

22. They know success in life is their energy, not their IQ.

So they optimize for high energy. They work out. They hang around high energy people. They eat the right food. And they go to bed early.

Writer Sahil Bloom says:

Your entire life will change when you realize energy is the most attractive human trait. Not looks, wealth, or status. Energy. Start walking into rooms with genuine enthusiasm, curiosity, and interest. Watch what happens. You become a magnet for the highest quality people. Energy is contagious. Spread the kind you’d want to catch.

People buy energy... they just can’t explain it. High energy creates extreme aura.

23. They are ruthless at follow up

No ask happens once.

They ask a 100 times. If they get ghosted, they just get other people to ask for them. If they still can't gain access, they show up randomly in person.

When I worked in consulting I had a banking client that wouldn’t take my calls. They discriminated against my employer because we were an Indian-based company. I decided not to get mad.

Instead, because we were an approved contractor, I got an access card to the building where all the decision-makers worked. I rolled up one morning at 7AM and sat in the middle of their open-plan office. I was a total stranger.

I made it a habit to be in all their meetings, eat lunch with them, and told them there was zero chance I'd be ignored. At the start, they thought I was weird. They didn’t like me. Within a few weeks I earned their respect.

They could tell I wasn’t f*cking around and would go to extremes to follow up and make stuff happen. They later signed a massive contract with me. My employer was blown away. No one was able to get past the cultural barrier. Except me. And I’m average IQ.

There is no such thing as no. Only a forced chance encounter.

Assume your first no isn't rejection.

24. They have a habit of getting rejected at least once a day.

The rejection muscle is trained because it’s what allows them to outperform later on.

Rejection is just redirection.

25. They can dance between chaos and order

One tragic event doesn’t throw them off.

They expect chaos and plan for it. They can act through challenging times. Their high performance life is a series of non-negotiable habits.

Without chaos there isn’t opportunity. The world runs on entropy and it must be embraced to be harnessed.

My LinkedIn Playbook

items.title: Technical writing in the age of AI
items.summary:
(Inspiration for this post was The Safest Job from AI may be Writing)

Replacing technical writers with AI agents writing documentation partially fails because there is no equivalent to software tests for documentation. There are some documentation testing frameworks, e.g. Doc Detective, and you can test parts of your documentation, but it’s not equivalent to code tests, which has more extensive testing and different testing types (unit tests, integration tests, regression tests).

You can generate slop code and test the outputs, and if the outputs are good, the code works and is therefore “good”, however sloppy it might otherwise be. (In domains where scalability, speed of execution, correctness in specific edge cases, and other such attributes are important, the code may not work because you cannot write a test for some of these requirements.) You can’t (fully) do the same thing with docs. You generate slop docs and…? Are they correct? Do they work, for any definition of “work”? Nobody knows. To check, someone would have to go through the steps and fail/succeed, at which point you’re doing technical writing.

Moreover, experiencing documentation means reading it, regardless of whether or not the reader achieves some objective. This is different from code: an end user interacts with code through an interface (a graphical one, or an API/contract) and therefore doesn’t necessarily need to interact with the logic that drives the mechanism of the code. They just need to send an input and receive an output. Even sloppy code is acceptable to the end user if it returns the desired result.

Compare that to documentation where the end user is required to read it: reading is interacting, the text of the documentation is the API. Writing style, conciseness, having a model of the reader, and so on, are all more important for documentation than for code, even if in the end, the reader accomplishes their goal regardless of the sloppiness or non-sloppiness of the documentation.

Finally, documentation carries with itself an implicit promise that a) there is someone who understands the subject matter, the issues, and how they were solved, and b) that this someone has decided to put their thoughts on paper teaching the reader and explaining to them different aspects of the problem-space and the solutions, and how one can use the created software artifacts to resolve the problems.

However, I concede that this last reason would also apply to code, and that it doesn’t really apply to the documentation in practice, and that this implicit promise has been broken more than kept. This is a standard of professionalism of yore, something that no longer applies in many cases, an erosion of trust and culture, at least to the extent that there ever was a time when professionals took pride in their craft and did in fact take part in this social contract of documentation.

And if I am being equally pragmatic, then this erosion extends to style, clarity, conciseness, all attributes listed in my 2nd point. If the end user ends up getting to the same result while reading bad prose in the same way as an end user who got to that result while reading good prose, good prose is somewhat irrelevant, though not fully irrelevant. It’s the same kind of irrelevance that happens when you have cringe AI-generated visuals. For some businesses, it really may be irrelevant, their relevant metrics will go up despite having bad taste. For others, there may be a financial cost associated with bad taste, and with poor prose.

There are also different aspects of (technical) writing. If you take the standard Diataxis division, AI is pretty good at building references. You can probably fully automate that and have your technical writers forget that they ever worked with code annotations or API reference generation. When it comes to how-to guides, that depends on the domain. Current agents are good at writing quick start guides for e.g. performing an initial API call, stuff like that. The more subject matter expertise required for a how-to guide, the worse agents will perform. For tutorials, I’m not sure, I think that agents work well for building introductions but given that they don’t really have a developed taste or have a model of the reader in their mind, I am skeptical of their success in the tutorial quadrant. Finally, in the explanation quadrant I think that they are very bad unless there’s a written record of trial and error during the design stage. Explanations are basically architectural records and are a mix of a bunch of things, so I guess that if an agent designed a thing from scratch, did its own iteration (trial and error), and saved all of its thinking traces somewhere, then I could see good explanations coming from agents. Otherwise they’d be inventing, and you don’t want any inventions in an explanation, you want someone to give you an overview of the problem space and how it was ultimately solved.

And all that is for technical writing in one of the four Diataxis quadrants. There’s also other technical or technical-adjacent writing. For example, explaining a design philosophy, or explaining a subject where the author collected expertise through a number of years, where there’s a lot of tacit knowledge that hasn’t been fully integrated in an agent’s training data. Or the genre of takes, where you basically never want to read an agent’s take on anything, as the whole point is to read the opinion of other humans, and rely on agents to be tools to perform actions.

items.title: Your entire life changes when you realize 99% of society is stupid
items.content_html:
Share

The title sounds like the most rude and entitled thing someone could ever say.

I’m prepared for the hell I may have unleashed. The “you privileged a**hole” or the “you think you’re so good, Tim Denning” comments. But as always, the shallow thinkers will trip themselves up and hang their own noose without me doing anything.

There is a deeper idea behind the somewhat controversial framing of the title that will change how you think about the life games you’re playing. It’s so rewarding for you that I’m willing to risk looking like a d*ck to help you understand it.

Here we go.

The statistics that don’t lie

It makes sense to consider IQ first.

IQ is built so that 100 is the exact average, and about 68% of people land between 85 and 115. So by that measurement 99% of people aren’t stupid based on IQ. But IQ isn’t a good measurement for stupidity.

A normal person can have a healthy IQ, but what can make them stupid is a lack of curiosity, excessive conformity, unexamined thinking, or conforming to beliefs as if they’re the only way which they inherited from a 3rd-party they never questioned.

The best example I can think of is a religious person I dated who joined a cult and never thought to question that everything the cult told them was in the cult’s best interest and not theirs. There was no reasoning with her. There was 100% an afterlife that she would get to live, but she couldn’t prove it. A guy just said so. “Trust me, bro.”

This is pure stupidity.

Again, statistically, most people follow the traditional path. They join an education system designed for factory workers, they get into huge debt for a degree, and they work a job they find boring after a year. Then they stay on this path until 65 and retire which is when they’re told to start living.

In case you think I’m special, I’m not.

I managed to skip the degree because my family couldn’t afford it, but I didn’t skip the traditional path. I got stuck there for over a decade in corporate hell.

That’s why I’m qualified to write about this topic because I was as stupid as it gets. And yes, I joined a dumb religious cult too for a while so I was also easy to brainwash.

Making it out of stupid society is the real prize. Stupid society is where most of us start, but we don’t need to stay there.

The modern amplifier of stupidity (that is your greatest opportunity)

I’m not sure if you’ve noticed, but society has gotten stupider in the last 5 years.

Two changes have happened:

  1. People spend most of their day looking at their phone screen and pinging their brain to death with notifications.

  2. People have outsourced some or even most of their thinking to AI platforms like Gemini, Claude, and ChatGPT.

Most people are accidentally living like robots, which is why their lives feel lifeless.

If we take the compassionate approach here, it’s not too far-fetched to say that if people are glued to a phone screen for most of their days and don’t do much of their own thinking anymore, it’s reasonable to assume we’d become stupider.

Algorithms run the platforms we use, we’re more distracted than ever, and we have access to infinite infotainment and entertainment.

The modern term for this state of living is called brainrot. Human brains are literally rotting from all the AI slop, context switching, high screen time, and lack of thinking.

So if we live like mindless robots as the default, then of course society is getting stupider, and obviously most (99%) people now meet the definition of stupid.

Suddenly, nothing in this essay is controversial at all. And it’s not meant to be.

The trend change no one could have ever predicted

(Not even me.)

No one trusts big corporations anymore. They’ve lied to us for too long.

This started in 2020 when 1000s of massive corporations, that told us they loved us and had smiling-assassin HR teams, suddenly began mass laying off people right when they needed their jobs the most during a bat virus that locked us in our homes.

I lived through this moment in history and it was jarring.

For the first time corporations were exposed as the wolf in sheep’s clothing that they’ve been all along. The costume came off. We saw the truth.

Since then there has been a quiet shift in sentiment.

More people are realizing no corporation gives a f*ck about them, and they’re a disposable human working on a temporary project. They’re also underpaid so their employer can make the maximum profit off of their work.

Now the default path starts to look more like the stupid path for a lot of us.

We’ve trusted our livelihoods and the ability to feed our families on a false god. Some people have continued to be lied to because it’s easier, and others, like me, have decided to accept the inconvenient truth.

Human psychology ruins us every time like death by a 1000 paper cuts

If you define stupidity based on what we do, then you realize that not doing stuff is a big part of the problem. Why don’t we do stuff? You’re going to hate my answer: a lack of self-improvement.

Every goal or how-to in any field boils down to the cookie-cutter basics of self-improvement that are so cliche at this point in history that I feel disgusting and like I need to have a shower for sharing them here with you.

For humans to NOT be lazy & stupid and get stuff done, they must: make their goals daily habits, have the right mindset (optimism), record their results, hang around others with similar goals, take action daily, and learn from those who have already achieved a similar goal. There you go… that’s my Jim Rohn speech from 1970.

It’s so simple yet no one does it.

Society is stupid because they don’t practice the basics of self-improvement. Instead, they rely on hope, luck, fantasies, waiting for the right time, or inconsistent levels of action. Without self-improvement our monkey brain runs on survival mode and destroys any chance we have of achieving anything.

The crazy part is every single person knows about the basics of self-improvement.

But knowing isn’t the same as doing. And doing it is hard some days, so it’s easier to not do it at all and either delude yourself into believing you are doing it, or to tell yourself you’ll start doing it when the chaos passes or the timing is right.

The viral meme that holds the simple answer

If we agree that 99% of society are stupid because of the way they act, and that most of us start out on a path that makes us part of the stupidity….

… then the answer is to do the opposite of 99% of people.

This has become a viral meme because, like all comedy, underneath it hides the truth.

  • If the average person works a job, you explore alternate work types – contracting, consulting, business ownership, freelancing, etc.

  • If the average person looks at their phone all day, you set up a system that makes sure you don’t look at your phone all day.

  • If the average person pings their brain to death all day with notifications, you turn off all notifications as your new default.

  • If the average person outsources all of their thinking to AI and hangs on every word an artificial brain tells them (sourced from 101 SEO content), you do all your own thinking and use AI as an amplifier for thinking, not a replacement for thinking.

  • If the average person gets underpaid for their skills and experience, you make your focus on earning multiple income streams from multiple customers instead of having one customer (an employer).

  • If the average person is lazy and comes home and watches Netflix every night to numb themselves, you use your free time to think, learn, grow, and be family-first.

  • If the average person uses holidays and weekends to escape their boring life, you make your focus to create a life you don’t feel the need to escape from.

  • If the average person is overweight and high on sugar, you make sure you exercise daily and eat real foods that aren’t made solely from chemicals.

The big idea is doing what most people do takes you down a dark path. If you choose the default option you get the default intelligence and results that come with it.

But you can rebel. You can resist.

You’re in control and you can just do things because 99% of society is too distracted or lazy to stop you.

The next big idea to wake you the hell up

A lot of us secretly don’t pursue our dreams because deep down we believe the market is saturated or there’s too much competition. This is a rational thought, but it’s bullsh*t if you’ve read everything I said above.

There is no competition. The market is stupid. They’re looking at their phones. They give up easily. They chase dopamine spikes. They binge on infotainment. They think short-term, and won’t do anything for 5 years.

So this is the big opportunity for you. If all the competition was imaginary from the start, what could you actually achieve? Answer: a lot.

Without competition life suddenly looks a lot easier. The barriers to entry seem low or even non-existent. And your entire life starts to look like a video game you can win if you just play on easy mode for a while.

This was the breakthrough I had about 5 years ago. I expected there would be all these people online writing their thoughts down, posting them, building email lists, selling simple products & services, and making it hard for me to succeed.

That hasn’t been the case at all. I can barely name any competition.

And that competition has been at it for less than a year, not 12 years like me. For the entire time I’ve been doing this, I expected smart people to outrun me. I thought the market would get sophisticated and posting stuff online would become impossible.

That didn’t happen at all. People just got more distracted with shiny objects as technology got better, instead of getting further ahead with the new tools.

Same applies to you.

The most dangerous place to be isn’t rock bottom. It’s the middle. Comfortable. Fine. Nothing is on fire – Dan Koe

What this all means for you

You don’t have to be part of mainstream stupidity.

You can escape the default path, think for yourself, and do the basics of self-improvement to avoid stupidity hell. But I want you to win even bigger. And I want to guarantee there’s almost no chance you lose.

To do so, it’s best you start thinking and acting like a leader. There’s a shortage of them right now. It’s also an easier path to get ahead. To be a leader and achieve your goals, you will need a tiny bit of courage every day.

You won’t be able to avoid hard conversations, ghost people, stay in indecision, or run a faceless social media account. You can’t worry about what people think either because you don’t have mind control powers to shape what people think about you.

The last thing you must do is question everything. Assume every idea or belief you hold in your mind might be wrong or at the very least defective. Assume the next level of life will be the result of how you think above all else.

This psychological programming will prepare you for change. This is crucial because the average person stays where they are because they’re terrible at dealing with change. That can’t be you. Change must be your best friend. It must be the default.

If you implement these last few things, the deck will be stacked so high in your favor, that it’ll be hard to lose. The statistical chance your theoretical competition does all this is less than 0.1%. Decent odds if you ask me.

PS

A lot of (stupid) people are shouting about the death of social media.

As usual, they are wrong.

But there’s a catch

You DO need a solid strategy for social.
